en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You've had your alone time. Tell me what's next.

speaker: Hekate
en: You're keeping up. Good. There's one more place we must weaken Persephone before our time together draws to a close. Her most devoted followers are gathering in a villa near Persephone's Embrace. These are the most vile humans in Elysium that serve her every whim and dark desire.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Are they under her possession?

speaker: Hekate
en: You might say they're more obsessed than possessed. But if you're thinking you can save these humans, you're sorely mistaken. Persephone's hold on them is too strong.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Until now, you've been helping humans, not hurting them.

speaker: Hekate
en: I'm helping people who help us and hurting people who stand in our way. Try to stay with me, won't you?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Whatever gets us closer to bringing down Persephone.

speaker: Hekate
en: I'm glad you see reason.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So what do you have in mind for Persephone's followers?

speaker: Hekate
en: Poison in their wine should do the trick. Unfortunately, the wolf nearby ate the last of my aconite. You'll need to hunt it and extract the poison from its liver. The symposium shouldn't be too difficult to infiltrate, but once you're there, try to blend in with the other Persephone-obsessed humans.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Adonis mentioned having rebel spies that attend similar events.

speaker: Hekate
en: Ah. Then you might want to warn such a spy not to drink the wine. I'm sure Adonis gave you a code to tell the spy you're an ally.

speaker: Kassandra
en: He did. Any idea what the spy might look like?

speaker: Hekate
en: From what I've heard, these spies tend to be middle-aged men wearing floral patterns and with animal motifs on their jewelry. A little obvious if you ask me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll find the poison and infiltrate the symposium.

speaker: Hekate
en: Don't worry, there'll be plenty of time to leave once the humans start drinking. Good luck.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Here it is.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's the poison. Now I've got a symposium to attend. Another one.

speaker: Leader of Devotees
en: A fresh face! Is this your first time at a Devoted Followers symposium?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Er, yes.

speaker: Leader of Devotees
en: Don't look so nervous, friend! Why don't you go meet some people, and then we'll toast to our new arrivals. Oh! If you're at a loss for words, let other members know whether you think Adonis or Hermes is Persephone's soulmate. We debate that for hours here.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Tell me, stranger. Who do you think Persephone's soulmate is? The god or the human?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Hermes. He clearly adores Persephone.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Thank the gods, someone here with some sense. Hermes doesn't get his due. He would follow Persephone to the end of the underworld.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Adonis. Persephone adores him.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: A while ago I would have agreed with you but... everyone knows Adonis has been slumming it with some human lately. Persephone deserves better.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Praise Persephone, friend.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Who spies and kills for Persephone? Is it your group?

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: What? No! Persephone would never want that. I think you're in the wrong place.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I should go meet more people.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Violets only bloom in Elysium winters.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Persephone's favorite flowers are poppies. Everyone knows that.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Persephone sent Adonis the most beautiful boat after he destroyed yet another felucca trying to escape Elysium.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: When will that ridiculous man realize Persephone is perfect for him?

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Enjoying the symposium?

speaker: Kassandra
en: So what do Persephone's Devoted Followers do?

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: For fun? We discuss the latest events in Persephone's life, plan symposiums, organize monuments in Persephone's honor...

speaker: Kassandra
en: I should be going.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Violets only bloom in Elysium winters.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: I... think you may have me confused with someone else.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Settle an argument, friend. We just got word that Persephone is expanding her palace. Should she build into the east or west of Elysium?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Only the best for Persephone, so... east.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: What? No! There's nothing for her to see in the east. What's she going to stare at, Hekate's hovel? That makes no sense.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I think she should expand west.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Thank you! If she wants a view of all the Minoan architecture, she must add a wing in the west.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Did you hear that Persephone refused Hades an invitation to her upcoming divine symposium?

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Why wouldn't she? He's her captor.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Having a good time?

speaker: Kassandra
en: How exclusive is this group?

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Not at all. We welcome new faces with open arms. Anyone who's willing to discuss Persephone all day long can join.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Enjoy the party.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Violets only bloom in Elysium winters.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Cold as Hades' heart.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Whatever you do, don't drink the wine.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: I know they're old rumors, but what do you think of the whispers that Hekate seeks to steal Persephone's throne for herself?

speaker: Kassandra
en: They look like good friends to me.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: You know, I completely agree. Persephone needs someone like Hekate by her side supporting her.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Anyone who can't see that Hekate is trying to rule Elysium herself is blind.

speaker: Persephone Devotee
en: Persephone? Blind? How could you say such a thing? She has molded Elysium into paradise. She's a visionary.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm ready for the toast.

speaker: Leader of Devotees
en: You know, everyone is saying what a great conversationalist you are. So knowledgeable about Persephone. You'll be a perfect fit here.

speaker: Kassandra
en: These people don't really seem as corrupt as Hekate made them out to be.

speaker: Leader of Devotees
en: Everyone gather to toast our new members.

speaker: Kassandra
en: To Persephone!

speaker: Leader of Devotees
en: To Persephone!

speaker: Kassandra
en: What? Hekate said it would take time to sink in. I'd better get out of here before

speaker: Kassandra
en: Wait! The wine was, er, well... I poisoned it.

speaker: Leader of Devotees
en: After we welcomed you so warmly? You're no friend! Guards!

speaker: Leader of Devotees
en: Oh, friend. Did you really think we wouldn't notice you tampering with our drinks? And after we welcomed you with open arms. Guards!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Hekate owes me answers. The symposium wasn't at all what I expected.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Why do I get the feeling I've been played?

speaker: Kassandra
en: This is the place. Time to burn some cargo.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Come and get it.

speaker: Brasidas
en: You fight like a Spartan! There's resolve in you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: We have that in common.

speaker: Brasidas
en: I saw innocents trapped in the flames.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The ones in the warehouse? I freed them already.

speaker: Brasidas
en: A good soldier acts when he's told. A great one is two steps ahead. Thank you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I did what I could. The flames were thick.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Not everyone can be spared of Hades. My thanks anyways.

speaker: Kassandra
en: My name's Kassandra. I'd thank you too if I knew who you were.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Brasidas of Sparta. You're a newcomer to Korinth.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're a spy too?

speaker: Brasidas
en: An old Spartan tactic. I have my ways.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I get the sense that's a Korinthian hobby. Anthousa has her hetaerae watching from every post.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Ah, Anthousa. We disagree, but have a common enemy.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The Monger?

speaker: Brasidas
en: We agree he should be killed, but we differ on how.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So, Sparta also has a Monger problem. What do you know about him?

speaker: Brasidas
en: His weapon has a far reach. Korinth is allied with Sparta. It's our duty to protect them.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then working alongside Anthousa is your best bet.

speaker: Brasidas
en: If she had her way, the Monger would be flayed in the streets. Sparta wants him dealt with quietly.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What do you want to do with him?

speaker: Brasidas
en: Right now, the Monger rules Korinth. I want to replace him with minimal bloodshed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: He'll only be dethroned if he's killed. It's simple.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Yes, diplomacy isn't something he understands.

speaker: Kassandra
en: From what I hear, I'm not surprised.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Killing him and his men doesn't seem to fit your peaceful proposal.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Nothing else has been successful. Trust me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What happened?

speaker: Brasidas
en: We arrested his top men. Armed the citizens. Tried to stir the polis against him. It never came to be. The only thing left to try

speaker: Brasidas
en: is a quick slice of the blade.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That would do it.

speaker: Brasidas
en: We'd lure him into Korinthia's Sacred Cave, and it'd be over.

speaker: Kassandra
en: By the time I leave Korinthia, the Monger will be dead.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Do that, and Sparta will be in your debt.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Anthousa has given me her word, and I've given her mine. She's hired me to kill the Monger.

speaker: Brasidas
en: She did?

speaker: Kassandra
en: She has something I need, and the Monger's in my way.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Keep your spear pointed his way, and Sparta will thank you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I was Spartan once.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Once?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Until I was thrown off Mount Taygetos as a child and left for dead.

speaker: Brasidas
en: You're the daughter of General Nikolaos? All of Sparta knows your name! And here you are—alive—impossible.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I survived. I raised myself alone while life continued in Sparta.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Never mind being a Spartan. Those of good character will forgive, and should be forgiven.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm on the hunt for my mother, Myrrine, and the only way is through Anthousa.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Yes. Myrrine.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You knew Nikolaos.

speaker: Brasidas
en: A good general, but a stubborn Spartan.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And rewarded for his loyalty.

speaker: Brasidas
en: But he disappeared, and his body was never found. The state pronounced him dead.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's all right. I haven't seen him since I was a child.

speaker: Brasidas
en: Devoted to Sparta until the end. I'm sorry. You heard of his death?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I did. A shame.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You don't know anything about Myrrine, do you?

speaker: Brasidas
en: I know that no one should have to endure such tragedy alone. And I heard she left Sparta that night. No one has forgotten Myrrine.

speaker: Kassandra
en: From what I know, she wanted them to forget.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's no going back now.

speaker: Brasidas
en: The displaced can always find their way home. The gods have just decided you must fight for it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: They couldn't make it any easier?

speaker: Brasidas
en: Chin up, Spartan. Easy doesn't exist.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Goodbye, Brasidas.

speaker: Brasidas
en: We'll meet again. I'm in the fight with you. Show courage.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Could be one of Stentor's scouts. Looks like he's run into problems.

speaker: Dolios
en: I'll gut every last Athenian responsible for this. Fucking cowards. Once they're dead, Stentor will know I'm worthy of fighting by his side.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What happened here?

speaker: Dolios
en: What business is it of yours, misthios? Do you know anything about this?

speaker: Kassandra
en: If I did, you'd already be dead. But it's your lucky day, I'm here to help. Stentor sent me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm a professional and a friend.

speaker: Dolios
en: What's that supposed to mean?

speaker: Kassandra
en: If it had been me, I'd have been smart enough to try and hide the evidence.

speaker: Dolios
en: Fair point. Whoever did this was brazen and foolish... Leaving it to be so easily discovered.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Or they wanted to send a message.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Stentor sent me. I'm here to help wherever I can.

speaker: Dolios
en: Stentor sent you?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sparta doesn't fully control Megaris... yet. It's easier for me to move freely in certain areas of Megaris than a Spartan.

speaker: Dolios
en: The Athenians have proven more resilient here than expected, but they will not stand...

speaker: Kassandra
en: ...Before Sparta, yes—I've heard the speeches. But until that glorious day comes, we should find out what happened here.

speaker: Dolios
en: Do you have any ideas?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Not yet but I will. I should get a closer look to figure out what happened here.

speaker: Kassandra
en: These were professional soldiers, slaughtered to a man. I don't think bandits could have done this...

speaker: Kassandra
en: The supplies are missing. They can't have gone far though... they didn't use the carts.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Looks like they went this way into the forest. I don't think I'll find anything else. I should report back.

speaker: Dolios
en: So was it the Athenians?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I found some fragments of green crystal...

speaker: Dolios
en: Bandits then! The mountains here are riddled with caves, and the war has made them brazen.

speaker: Kassandra
en: If it was Athenians, they would have taken the carts as well as the supplies... And bandits, they wouldn't have stood a chance against trained Spartans.

speaker: Dolios
en: What are you saying?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Nothing about this adds up...

speaker: Dolios
en: In what way?

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's no bodies, at least not any assailants. Athenians would have taken the carts and their dead, but bandits would have left their fallen in the dust.

speaker: Dolios
en: Then who did it?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm not sure. Whoever did this went into the forest... So I'll start by looking there.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's food being cooked near here. There they are!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Is this a private gathering, or can anyone join?

speaker: Neaera
en: Wha... What are y... Please, please just leave.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You don't look like murderers, was that the Spartans' mistake?

speaker: Neaera
en: What? Wait! No, please you don't understand!

speaker: Kassandra
en: What's to understand? It all seems perfectly clear.

speaker: Neaera
en: Please, let me plead our case?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You'd better tell me why I shouldn't just kill you and return the goods.

speaker: Neaera
en: Please, I'll tell you anything you want to know.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're the sorriest band of thieves I've ever seen.

speaker: Neaera
en: By the gods, no! We're citizens of Megara. Please, show mercy. This war has already cost us dearly.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Like the mercy you showed those Spartan soldiers?

speaker: Neaera
en: I, we... We just took some food. Hyrkanos told us to take it, said he'd make it easy for us.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Hyrkanos?

speaker: Neaera
en: Yes, the mercenary. He said he'd provide food, told us the Athenians would never let their people go hungry.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Explain yourselves! It's not wise to anger the Spartans.

speaker: Neaera
en: Please, we're not thieves. This is our food, our crops. They took it, left us with nothing! Our children are starving...

speaker: Kassandra
en: So you repay theft with murder? A fine lesson for your children.

speaker: Neaera
en: Murder, no. Please, we never harmed anyone.

speaker: Civilian
en: A misthios told us where to find the food. Everyone was already dead!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Enough, I didn't come here for debate. It's too late for talk now. I came to find who's behind this crime against Sparta.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Stand aside, you don't need to die today. I'm returning the supplies to the Spartans.

speaker: Neaera
en: Then you will do so over our dead bodies!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Don't be stupid. Take some of the food, enough to get by. I'll say I killed you and claimed what was left. They will be satisfied.

speaker: Neaera
en: But the food, what of our families?!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your families will not benefit from your death. Accept my offer and don't steal again. It won't be me who comes for you next time.

speaker: Neaera
en: Yes, misthios... Thank you. Hurry! Take what you can carry and go. Quick.

speaker: Dolios
en: Kassandra Did you find the ones responsible?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I found your supplies with a bunch of hungry Megarians.

speaker: Dolios
en: And?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You stole that food from them. They were starving.

speaker: Dolios
en: The supplies were essential for the war and ridding Megara of the Athenians.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Hungry Megarians are the least of your worries, but there's something else. Have you heard of a mercenary called Hyrkanos?

speaker: Dolios
en: Hyrkanos... Yes, he is working for the Athenians, so the rumours go.

speaker: Kassandra
en: This is all his doing.

speaker: Dolios
en: These mercenaries are persistent, I'll give them that. You've done well here, but if you really want to help Sparta, I have a task for you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What do you have in mind?

speaker: Dolios
en: Hunt him down! Show him that no mercenary dog will interfere with Sparta's plans.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Since you have such a high opinion of mercenaries, why even send me?

speaker: Dolios
en: I'm sorry... It's just this man Hyrkanos is like a thorn in our foot. He's a menace to all Spartans here. Please, will you help us?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll do it. If he's this much trouble, I take it there's a sizeable reward?

speaker: Dolios
en: Of course! Just think of how much he'll have on him with all the drachmae Athens have given him to thwart our plans.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I suppose you're right... Any idea where to start looking?

speaker: Dolios
en: He could be anywhere. Most likely, he's nestled up close to the Athenians. We've sent out a couple of patrols, but they never returned, and we can't spare any more men at this time.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sometimes you're better sending a woman, anyway.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There is only one just punishment for your crime.

speaker: Civilian
en: It was our food to begin with!

speaker: Neaera
en: We either die here by your hand, or slowly starve later...If I'm to die, I would rather die fighting.

speaker: Dolios
en: Kassandra! Did you find the ones responsible?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I found your supplies with a bunch of hungry Megarians.

speaker: Dolios
en: And?

speaker: Kassandra
en: They won't trouble you again.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You are murderers and thieves, and deserve no better.

speaker: Neaera
en: Please, no! You don't understand, it was a mercenary that killed the soldiers!

speaker: Neaera
en: Please, no!

speaker: Civilian
en: Mercenaries attacked the wagons, not us!

speaker: Neaera
en: We were just hungry...

speaker: Dolios
en: Kassandra! Did you find the ones responsible?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I found your supplies with a bunch of hungry Megarians.

speaker: Dolios
en: And?

speaker: Kassandra
en: They won't trouble you again.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Can I help you, merchant?

speaker: Woman
en: You! Oh, my husband told me about how you spared his life in the fishing district.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Well, your husband could have been in a lot of trouble threatening a man like the politician Metiochos, but I know he and his friends meant well.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your husband should be more careful. He and his friends could have gotten in a lot of trouble threatening the politician Metiochos.

speaker: Woman
en: Of course, you're right. But he took your advice, and a bunch of us Athenians have gotten together to help the fishing district... and now we need your help again, too.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm listening.

speaker: Woman
en: I'm too busy tending my stall, but I need to deliver these new sandals made for a local beggar. We have a clothing drive here now. See? I told you we're turning things around. All thanks to you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And you want me to deliver it to him.

speaker: Woman
en: Yes, simple enough. It needs to arrive in one piece.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm in.

speaker: Woman
en: You're a gods-send.

speaker: Kassandra
en: We're done here.

speaker: Kassandra
en: A merchant told me you'd want this.

speaker: Man
en: Perfect timing, misthios. Let me repay you.

speaker: Power Corrupts All
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan in 2018 through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: My, my, is that Kassandra of Agiad? The Eagle Bearer? Messenger of Zeus? She who launched a thousand hearts?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Alkibiades, I am known by many names, but that last one sounds to be of your own making.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: My young friend Orchimedes here could use your legendary talents to woo the object of his desire.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: You would have my eternal gratitude.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: I'm Orchimedes, I came to Alkibiades because he boasts of his exploits as a lover and knows Praxilla.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm a misthios, not some famed lover.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: I heard that Kassandra learned a special healing touch from Lykaon.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Nonsense! She proved her strength, dexterity, and endurance when she got Roxana on her back.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Nonsense! I've heard that our misthios here is the only one allowed near the pirate queen Xenia's booty.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Have you ever heard of Praxilla?

speaker: Kassandra
en: The name sounds familiar. Who is she?

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Who is she? A poet blessed by Apollo himself! She describes the gods as if they were her lovers. Her lyre is a legendary weapon, wielded in her hands. I want to meet her, but talking to a goddess such as she... terrifying.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Oh nonsense, usually you give a woman some flowers and she'll show you her flower. However, this is Praxilla. She is not easily impressed.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Of course, no ordinary flower will do. They need to be worthy of a goddess.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: I come to this coast every year for the poetry festival. Of all the beautiful blossoms, none match the scent and radiance of the Coral Rose. Fetch some, and all doors and legs shall open for you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll return with your flowers.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Where can I find the Coral Rose? It sounds rare.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: You would be correct. However, like all good things in life, these take more work than most are willing to expend. They're atop a nearby mountain.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Say I do get these flowers... Where would I bring them?

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Back to camp. Praxilla should be in her tent.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You mentioned being here for a poetry festival?

speaker: Alkibiades
en: I did! It's one of the many festivals to Apollo, but this one holds a special place in my heart, among other places. Other festivals are so stuffy. Here, we worship like maenads.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've heard enough.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Please, if you are as skilled with sword and heart as Alkibiades says, you'll return to me with the Coral Rose. As a poet, it's best that I stay at camp while you do the hiking.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You'd be an easy snack for wolves or bears. I'll return with the roses.

speaker: Kassandra
en: These must be the Coral Roses.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've found your Coral Roses.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: You're back! That's... that's perfect. Those roses are perfect. Oh, look at the luster. The fragrance. Now, you must deliver them to her.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You came all this way to meet her. You should be the one to do it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's not what I was hired for. You give them to her.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Please! I'm much too nervous to speak to her. I've composed a poem to recite. Here, let me teach you

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'd say it all wrong. I'm a misthios, not a poet.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Then would you at least deliver the flowers while I rehearse?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Fine, but the rest is up to you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm not saying any malákas poem. That's your job, not mine.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Then I must rehearse. Will you at least deliver the flowers before they wilt?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Fine, but you'll do the rest.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: OK, she's at her tent. Right there. Go give them to her.

speaker: Praxilla
en: The misthios returns! Do you have the time to accompany me and Achaikos to our triumphant performance?

speaker: Kassandra
en: After all this, I wouldn't miss it.

speaker: Praxilla
en: Excellent, we team up once more.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So we're a team now? Can I still expect to get paid?

speaker: Praxilla
en: After my performance, drachmae will be in no short supply, trust me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You've dedicated your life to your art. You must have a lot to show for it.

speaker: Praxilla
en: I write a hundred poems every night when I go to sleep and throw out a hundred every morning when I wake up. Luckily some have survived to touch people.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Do you have any favorites?

speaker: Praxilla
en: There's one I'm well known for that is very dear to me. The most beautiful thing I leave is the light of the sun. Second are the shining stars and the face of the moon. Then ripe cucumbers, apples, and pears too.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sounds nice. But we should get going.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So, cucumbers?

speaker: Praxilla
en: The sun gives us the fruit of the trees like the fruit of the loins.

speaker: Kassandra
en: In your poem, you say you leave the sun. Why?

speaker: Praxilla
en: Not me. Adonis. He is being asked upon death about the most beautiful things he's left behind. To me, there is no greater beauty than that of the sun and the moon and stars.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Oh! Why is he being asked this?

speaker: Praxilla
en: Adonis is beauty incarnate. What could be so beautiful that even he would be pained to leave?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I see. Looks like we made it.

speaker: Praxilla
en: Marvelous, thank you! Looks like my adoring fans are ready for me. Be sure to catch the show.

speaker: Phaenna
en: It's Praxilla!

speaker: Laches
en: I heard she was coming this year!

speaker: Krantor
en: Praxilla! Recite something for us.

speaker: Praxilla
en: I've been reciting this poem for years. Kassandra, would you do me the kindness of allowing me to hear it anew from your lips?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I couldn't.

speaker: Praxilla
en: Nonsense, you know everything you need to do it justice. How about something new this year?

speaker: Kassandra
en: The most beautiful thing I leave is the light of the sun.

speaker: Krantor
en: Praise be Apollo!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Second are the shining stars and the face of the moon.

speaker: Laches
en: This is one of my favorites.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then ripe cucumbers, apples, and pears too.

speaker: Civilian
en: That's always been my favorite verse.

speaker: Praxilla
en: I'm happy my poem touched you so deeply, Kassandra. Have you thought about trading your spear for the lyre?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I will stick to swinging swords, thanks.

speaker: Praxilla
en: It wouldn't be a poetry festival without someone causing a disturbance.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Praxilla! Get to safety. I can handle them.

speaker: Praxilla
en: Happens every year. Some cursed idiots drink too much wine and get themselves killed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I didn't know poetry festivals were such lively events.

speaker: Praxilla
en: Indeed. I need to take a moment to recover. Let's go back to my tent.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Ah, but we do have a happy ending!

speaker: Orchimedes
en: Praxilla, it has taken me long years of soul searching and many nights of tears to bring myself to this moment. I am Orchimedes, your son.

speaker: Praxilla
en: When I heard the name of the man who stole my lyre, I suspected it might be you.

speaker: Orchimedes
en: I've dreamt of hurting you as you hurt me and my father a thousand times. But I only knew you as the mother who abandoned me, and not as the artist I just saw.

speaker: Praxilla
en: Just as Adonis lamented the beauty he left behind, I too left that which was most precious to me on the death of my old self.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're not dead. Neither of you are. Take this opportunity and see what you can build together.

speaker: Praxilla
en: Thank you for all your help.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I picked up your message on the board. What's happening?

speaker: Woman
en: A merchant's been robbed, misthios! He was supposed to sell a bridle to me today... I need it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then buy one from someone else. Why do you care that a merchant was robbed?

speaker: Woman
en: This bridle... It contains secret information about Sparta's next move, but bandits have it in their camp.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You want me to get it from the bandits?

speaker: Woman
en: That's exactly it. Will you do it for me?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll help you.

speaker: Woman
en: The gods are smiling on me, then.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Chaire.

speaker: Woman
en: Did you get it?

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's all yours.

speaker: Woman
en: Thank you for all you've done. Please, take this.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That'll do.

speaker: Precious Jewels
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Xenia
en: Still breathing?

speaker: Galateia
en: Everything hurts, so I guess so.

speaker: Xenia
en: Galateia limped home after her ship was attacked. She lost vital cargo, and several of her crew were taken prisoner. You could fix these problems for me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What do you need?

speaker: Xenia
en: Galateia, tell your story.

speaker: Galateia
en: We were sailing near Pellene, when we were ambushed. Our ship was boarded and sunk. I escaped, but I lost our prized cargo.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Who attacked you, and why?

speaker: Galateia
en: Soldiers of one faction or another. They are all the same to me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That doesn't make finding them easier.

speaker: Galateia
en: I was too busy holding in my guts to worry about what banner they were flying.

speaker: Xenia
en: Calm yourself. Galateia told me the thieving scum retreated to the Olouros Fortress.

speaker: Galateia
en: Yeah, in Achaia.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What did your crew lose that was so dear?

speaker: Galateia
en: A prized old coffer for Xenia.

speaker: Xenia
en: The exact what and why are not important. Only understand that the coffer carries something I value greatly. Bring it back, and I'll reward you well.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What happened to the rest of the crew?

speaker: Galateia
en: Many died in the fighting, but I saw at least three dragged off by the malákes.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And where were you?

speaker: Galateia
en: Bleeding in the surf, trying to make sure I did not go to the crows. So someone would live to tell the tale.

speaker: Xenia
en: Rest, Galateia. Among the missing are my master of maps, Anaximander, keen-eyed Iaira, and Galateia's brother, Kittos. They are all terribly loyal. It would be a shame to lose them.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Leave it to me. I'll find your crew and your precious cargo.

speaker: Xenia
en: West Wind, have you had any luck finding my lost cargo or my missing crew? Galateia said the tragedy occured near Olouros Fortress.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You must be Anaximander.

speaker: Anaximander
en: Eh, yes. How did you know?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've studied so many of your maps, I feel as if I know you.

speaker: Anaximander
en: Our precious cargo, Xenia's coffer, will be held in their treasury. Can you recover it?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I will.

speaker: Anaximander
en: May Poseidon shower you with fortune for saving me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Thank you. You should be safe now.

speaker: Old Coffer
en: This old coffer contains something of incalculable value to the pirate queen Xenia, chief of Keos.

speaker: Kassandra
en: This must be the coffer that Xenia covets.

speaker: Xenia
en: You recovered my coffer. Gratitude.

speaker: Xenia
en: Still, the loss of my crew hurts a great deal. It's harder to prize anything greater than the people you trust.

speaker: Xenia
en: You found the coffer and rescued my crew! I know you'll find it ridiculous, but this clay doll was a gift from my mother. A strong figure she was, tough as Hera and clever as Athena. She cared for us after my wretch of a father got himself lost or dead.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I... didn't expect that.

speaker: Xenia
en: No one is only one thing, my West Wind.

speaker: Kassandra
en: True...

speaker: Xenia
en: Enough chatter. I have another use for your tongue and your hands. Your skills are needed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Yes. I'll go down with you.

speaker: Xenia
en: Perfect. Let me show my private collection.

speaker: Xenia
en: Kassandra, your presence makes the day hot and sultry. I know I can never own the West Wind, but it pleases me that I was able to tame it for a little while.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I don't have time to breathe, let alone anything else. Glad you are happy with what I recovered, though.

speaker: Xenia
en: Gratitude, . You've done right by me.

speaker: Xenia
en: What could have been another life, my West Wind? I will always see the fire in your eyes reflected in the treasures you brought me. Farewell, Kassandra.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Spare some drachmae?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: You there. You have a kind soul. Help an old man buy this next meal?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your... soul also seems kind.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I am grateful and humbled, stranger. Tell me, what do they call you?

speaker: Kassandra
en: If you knew the things I've done, you wouldn't be so quick to call me kind.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Nonsense. Your soul is greater than the sum of your actions, stranger... Tell me, what do they call you?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You need it more than me. Here, take it.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: A generous gift. Thank you. What do they call you, stranger?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You and I have something in common. Neither of us has any drachmae.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Your company is gift enough, but... I don't know your name. Who do they call you?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm Kassandra. And you?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Depends on who's asking... But my name is Kassandra. And you are?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm the Messenger of Zeus. But you can call me Kassandra. And you are?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Just a simple beggar. I sailed from Persia to see the beauty of the Greek world.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I can do many things, Persian, but I can't restore sight.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Nor would I want you to. My blindness is a burden that the gods have given me to carry, and I will.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then what?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Be my eyes. When I was a boy, an Athenian told me the most beautiful of your lands. I would love to hear them again. Would you go to see the places I never was able to, and return to tell me the tale of your adventures?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm not much of a storyteller, but I will be your eyes.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I know I sensed kindess in you. You've made this old Persian happy again.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Don't thank me yet. What places do you wish you could have seen?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Ah, my favourite tales were always of the Akrokorinth, the statues of Zeus and Athena, the perch of the armored bird in Arkadia, and of course, the mysterious Mount Taygetos.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So, tell me what you know about the Statue of Zeus.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: "Its great bolt stood ready to punish the Kephallonias below," or so I was told.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There are many statues to Athena. Which one do you mean?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: In my mind, there is only one. Her story always began, "As we're rounded the hilltops, we could see Athens bustling below us, and Athena above, matching our gaze.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The Akrokorinth... Don't tell me, it's in Korinthia.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Smart guess. It is the most renowned temple to Aphrodite, your goddess of all life's most pleasurable trivialities.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You did say Mount Taygetos, didn't you?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: You sound like you know that place... I have heard tales of its appetites. They say the mountain feeds on the suffering of Spartans, so the people there offer their own children to the mountain god for sacrifice.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That... that's not exactly right.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What do you remember about this armored bird in Arkadia?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: There's a beast made of armor jutting out from the mountainside, overlooking Lake Stymphalos and the undulating fields stretching like waves on a golden sea all across Akradia.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll be back with stories to tell.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: As soon as you've seen one location, please return.

speaker: Kassandra
en: This papyrus is so old... Could this be writing by Themistokles?

speaker: Themistokles on Kephallonia
en: Zeus's mighty figure stood aloft, its great bolt ready to punish the Kephallonians below. This is how the Kephallonians were destined to live—under the shadow of a god always watching and ready to judge.

speaker: Kassandra
en: A papyrus. Says it was written by Themistokles, the Athenian general.

speaker: Themistokles on Athens
en: As we rounded the hilltops, we could see Athens bustling below us and Athena above, matching our gaze. There, she eternally mourned our suffering with dignity and grace.

speaker: Kassandra
en: A note... written by Themistokles. Who knew the great general was also a poet?

speaker: Themistokles on the Akrokorinth
en: No people on this earth were more dedicated to worship than the followers of Aphrodite. No matter the time, the men were worshipping with the women, and the women with the men, only stopping to sleep or drink.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've seen Kephallonia from the Statue of Zeus.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Tell me, is it still a place of great beauty?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Its people are the happiest in all the Greek world. They sing and dance into the night, with full bellies and full hearts.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: That... isn't how it was described to me at all. The tales go that its lands are among the world's most beautiful, and its people among the most pitiful.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Yes, the island is beautiful. From the Statue of Zeus, you can see the sea hitting the white beaches and mountains covered in green. But its people suffer because of the war.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Ah, just how it was described to me. The gods simultaneously bless the land and curse the people. Even for gods, your gods are cruel, misthios.

speaker: Kassandra
en: OK, I've told you what I remember. Now tell me about yourself. What's a Persian doing here?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Persia and the Greek world are doomed to be opposites—in times of prosperity here, Persians always seem to suffer. And when you are at war with yourselves

speaker: Kassandra
en: Persians know peace?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Indeed. My people prospered after King Xerxes was murdered. All except for me. A man tried to kill me with poison, which is how I lost my sight. I fled and arrived here.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I find it hard to believe anyone would want you dead.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: You're very kind. Tell me another tale, then I'll tell you more of my past.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So, there's a price on your head? Now I'm interested.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: There was, though there isn't anymore. Now then, tell me another tale, and I'll tell you more of my past.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You'll be glad to know I've been to the Statue of Athena at the Akropolis.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Ah, if only I could have been there to feel her prescence. Would you... describe her to me?

speaker: Kassandra
en: If Athens is a city of statues, then Athena is their guardian. She stands high above everything, on guard over the city.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Yes! Not just standing tall to protect Athens, but to serve as a reminder of the suffering those poor people endured during the invasion.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Oh, it's even better than you can imagine. Made of pure gold. Chip one toe off her, and you'd have enough drachmae to eat for the rest of your life.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Gold? No, it can't be. I was always told she was bronze, and stood guard over the city of Athens. Mourning the past and protecting the future...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your turn to tell me something. You said a man tried to kill you.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: The man who rose up to kill the tyrant Xerxes was named Darius... He was of a new creed of killers, unlike any Persia had known. He was also the man hired to kill me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: A killer of kings, hired to kill a simple blind man? Why?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I have your interest, do I? Tell another tale, and I will, too.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I traveled to the Akrokorinth. From there I could see all of Korinthia.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Ah! I can only wonder at what the worshippers of Aphrodite do to pay her tribute.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The hetaerae keep the spirit of Aphrodite alive... Usually well into the night.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Exactly as your goddess deserves! When I was younger, I'd lie awake dreaming of what it would be like to go... worship, of course.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's quiet, mostly. People praying, offering sacrifice. You know, typical sanctuary stuff.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: A temple to Aphrodite... quiet? Impossible! Have you ever been to the temple?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Now that's out of the way, you owe me a tale. You said the king killer, Darius, was hired to kill you, too.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: He was. By my brother.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your brother! None of this is making any sense, old man.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I trust you, so I will tell you. My brother and I are the last living sons of King Xerxes.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Impossible. That would make you king.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I was. My name was Artaxerxes. I guided Persia through a time of peace. But my brother wanted the throne and plotted my death. Now, I hide here, exiled, living the life of a simple beggar. I will tell you more, but first

speaker: Kassandra
en: Yes, yes. A tale for a tale.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I returned to Mount Taygetos.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Returned? Tell me, did you meet the mountain god who devours Spartan children?

speaker: Kassandra
en: The mountain is just a mountain like any other—what makes Taygetos a place of suffering is the people there.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: That is true of all the world's worst places. When I was a child... I could tell from the moment I met you that you carried the burden of suffering. Let it stay in the past.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your story was true—there is a snow god on Mount Taygetos that lives to eat the children of Sparta. It destroys families for fun. I saw it.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: That was a Persian myth, and a disgusting one—I had always hoped to heare the tale of the true Taygetos from someone who'd seen it firsthand.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Now you tell me, "King" Artaxerxes—how can I believe your story? You don't exactly look like royalty.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Well, that's the point. I am hiding.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Show me proof.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I could. You see, I knew a man named Themistokles.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The Athenian general. I heard stories about him being ostracized from Athens.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Over petty politics. He came to Persia, to me, looking for refuge. I was king, but only a boy. He spent his days learning Persian and telling me stories of his home. Places like that Akrokorinth, Mount Taygetos...

speaker: Kassandra
en: The palaces you wished you could see.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I loved the tales, and loved Themistokles like a father. He was kinder to me than Xerxes ever was. Tell me one last tale, and I'll tell you where he hid his treasure.

speaker: Kassandra
en: If you'd like to hear about the bird, I could describe it to you.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Nothing would make me happier.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The great bird with metal feathers attacked me. I fought it off with my bare hands.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: You did? So, you fought it just like Herakles? I'd heard the statue was built to guard a place of chaos and calm.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's a majestic statue, built from the blades of fallen soldiers. It is so high above Stymphalos and the golden fields below... Up there I could forget there was a war.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: So, it is as it was told to me. The bird commemorates Herakles' fight against chaos, built on a place of calm. Hopefully one draws out the best in the other.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So, I've been to the five places Themistokles told you in his tales.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: For that, my soul will be eternally grateful. As for my tale, Themistokles died peacefull in Persia, as one of us. I promised him I'd see the places he'd told me about. His stories will live on in me, and now you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And what of your story?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I let the people believe Darius succeeded in killing me so I could escape.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Artaxerxes... There's something else you should know.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Yes?

speaker: Kassandra
en: My grandfather was Leonidas of Sparta.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: That means...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your father, King Xerxes, killed my grandfather.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Then you're bounded by blood to avenge him.

speaker: Kassandra
en: On second though, never mind.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Kings, murderers, Athenian generals, adventure... You tell a good tale, old man.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: After all that, you don't believe me?

speaker: Kassanda
en: I think you're a great storyteller. It doesn't matter if any of it was true.

speaker: Persian Soldier
en: Artaxerxes! False king. This misthios led me right to you. Time to finish what I started.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Kassandra, please.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Stand behind me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Your father killed my grandfather. Now, I kill you.

speaker: Persian Soldier
en: No! He's mine.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Artaxerxes. Are you hurt?

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Despite being bound by honor to avenge Leonidas, you saved me. Thank you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I had no choice. That man wanted you dead... Must've been another one of your executioners.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: After a life as a Persian king, you get used to people trying to kill you.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: You call me by my name, despite accusing me of being a rambling old man. Now you believe me?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I do now. That killer was Persian... Another one of your brother's hired executioners.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: It was. If he doesn't return to Persia, my brother will send another. Then another. It's time this old man accepts his fate.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You are a brave man, Artaxerxes.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: A trait I learned from Themistokles. Now, as for you... I owe you payment.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Well, I did save your life. And I went on an adventure for you... your highness.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sure, you could give up. Or, you could sail home, kill your brother, and take back your kingdom.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: I spent my entire life undoing my father's work. I won't end my life becoming him. As for you... there is the matter of your payment.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Well, I did save your life. And I went on an adventure for you... your highness.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Before that, you owe me. I saved your life. And I went on this adventure for you.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: You did! And in your retelling, I felt like Themistokles was speaking through you. For your reward, go to the tomb in Salamis where Themistokles hid his treasure. It will be near where he made his triumphant stand against my father's navy.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: You did... Though much of what you said is not how I remember Themistokles telling it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Things change.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Ah, we are proof of that, aren't we? Now for Themistokles treasure. Find the tomb in Salamis, where he made his triumphant stand against my father's navy. That's where your reward awaits.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: Did you? Athena made from pure gold, meeting a god on Taygetos, and how did you describe the Akrokorinth? "Typical sanctuary stuff?"

speaker: Kassandra
en: You said you like stories. So... I gave you stories.

speaker: Artaxerxes
en: At least I'm still alive. For that, take this small token.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The tomb that Artaxerxes mentioned. It's real.

speaker: Kassandra
en: A small alleyway...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Chaire, Kleta.

speaker: Kleta
en: Misthios, you came. Thanks to you, these people are safe.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Call me Kassandra.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Looks like the stranded people are settling in well.

speaker: Kleta
en: Resources are scarce, but we make do with what we have. These people have nowhere to go. Marooned, alone, far from home... I try to provide them a little bit of comfort.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's normal to be uncomfortable—better, even. That's a principle of Spartan training. It's how they become such fierce warriors.

speaker: Kleta
en: You remind me of my daughter. She ways always aspiring to be better, to be greater.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's not aspiring if you're already great.

speaker: Kassandra
en: We all have things about ourselves that could be improved.

speaker: Kleta
en: These people will have to be their best selves if they're going to escape the Tempest. Her forces are monitoring the ships in and out of Achaia, and their control over the island is growing stronger everyday. We need to get them out of here. Will you help me, Kassandra?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll help. What do I need to do?

speaker: Kleta
en: Leaving Achaia is not going to be easy, but I've spoken to a few of the stranded and we've come up with a plan. Find Orontas. He's overlooking the fields. He'll have more information about this.

speaker: Orontas
en: Oh... They've flown away.

speaker: Orontas
en: Ah. A misthios. Tell me, is there anything more beautiful than this? The calm, the peace, the comfort of a simple life...

speaker: Kassandra
en: The idea of settling down is like a dream to me. I seem to go from one problem to the next.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The life of a mercenary is the life I want to live. I like to keep busy.

speaker: Orontas
en: In that case, welcome to Boura.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What brings you to Achaia?

speaker: Orontas
en: I've traveled across many seas, misthios. The blockade paused my journey as a merchant, but... Kleta gave me a place to stay. When you've been through as much as I have, when you've weathered the most horrific and turbulent storms... you start to appreciate the simple joys of life. Like Boura, a place I could call home.

speaker: Orontas
en: I fear these quiet times won't last.

speaker: Kassandra
en: All peace is hard earned. It should be treasured.

speaker: Orontas
en: My sentiments exactly.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've lived in chaos. I can show you a trick or two.

speaker: Orontas
en: I'm all ears.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Kleta sent me to you. She said you lost your ships.

speaker: Orontas
en: Indeed. We're in troubling times, misthios. Achaia is growing more dangerous by the day, and we need to escape while we can. I've discussed the plan at length with Kleta, and

speaker: Order Guard
en: Keep looking!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Guards!

speaker: Orontas
en: They've upped their patrols.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I caught their attention at the fort. They're looking for more stranded.

speaker: Orontas
en: We mustn't let them disrupt our peace, misthios. Deal with them quietly if you can. I'll get Kleta and the rest to higher ground.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I have to stop them before they get to the village.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Another one.

speaker: Greek Soldier
en: Be careful. Remember what happened at the fort.

speaker: Order Guard
en: Comb all the fields! Turn over every rock if you have to!

speaker: Guardian
en: We can't go back empty-handed. The Tempest won't be forgiving.

speaker: Greek Soldier
en: Oh no... What was that?

speaker: Hektor
en: They—they say she has the power of the gods.

speaker: Greek Soldier
en: Shut up.

speaker: Greek Soldier
en: There's the Eagle Bearer! After her!

speaker: Kassandra
en: More guards... On horseback!

speaker: Greek Soldier
en: You'll pay for what you did, misthios!

speaker: Orontas
en: Misthios, you prevailed.

speaker: Kleta
en: Thank you, Kassandra. I... I knew they were on the move, but I didn't think it'd be so soon.

speaker: Kleta
en: We need to set our plan in motion.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me what needs to be done.

speaker: Orontas
en: We need a mode of transport across the Aegean. The ships we came in were taken when we arrived in Boura by the foreman of the docks.

speaker: Kleta
en: Perhaps we can strike a deal with the foreman to get them back.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I have the time to help you now.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I have other things to do.

speaker: Kleta
en: Come back when you have time. We could use your help.

speaker: Kleta
en: In that case, we should bring you up to speed on the foreman situation.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm listening.

speaker: Kleta
en: He's quite a character, I've heard rumours that he frequents a tavern in Pellene and drinks as if to endlessly worship Dionysos. Word is he doesn't take well to mercenaries.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I can get people to like me.

speaker: Orontas
en: I'm sure you have your ways, misthios.

speaker: Kleta
en: My daughter... She always loved the water. As a girl, she always wanted to steer when we rowed out to sea. As she got older... I've never stopped wondering if she will come back to me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me more about your daughter.

speaker: Kleta

speaker: Kassandra
en: This is it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That must be Ampheres. Why so many guards?

speaker: Ampheres
en: Let her Pass.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Ampheres, if this is how you treat humans, I can see why you need so many guards.

speaker: Ampheres
en: These aren't humans. They are animals. And animals should be in cages.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Dead bodies of civilians outside. A tortured corpse at your feet. The only animal I see around here is you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm sure everything you do isn't without reason, but if you didn't call them animals, you might get a better reaction.

speaker: Ampheres
en: A human did this to me while I slept. When they came to kill me, I survived, but the slaughtered my daughter like an animal. Humans don't act with logic or reason.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Good or bad, they are driven by a will to survive.

speaker: Ampheres
en: A trait we implanted to ensure efficiency. But, that will become a kindled flame of insurrection. You led a rebellion yourself in Elysium, so I know you understand. If we don't act, the city will burn and many more lives will be lost.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I don't see an army marching on Poseidon.

speaker: Ampheres
en: This one said they plan to launch an attack. Someone needs to destroy the resistance before that happens.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's not a small request. Despite what you think, all humans aren't a threat.

speaker: Ampheres
en: It is the only path I see. But you are the Dikastes. Only you can choose the correct course of action.

speaker: Kassandra
en: If we find an kill the leaders - the ones spreading the message - the rest will lose interest.

speaker: Ampheres
en: An interesting theory. Perhaps you're right. If the leaders are removed, the rest may see the error of their opposition.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Killing people will just make the fire spread faster. If we destroy their supplies and their weapons, they can't oppose the Isu.

speaker: Ampheres
en: I admire your optimism, but i fear it will not be enough. However, it's your decision to make.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Just leave it to me. I'll send a message they won't forget.

speaker: Ampheres
en: Very well. You'll find the traitorous humans at an abandoned farmstead. Return to me when the situation is resolved

speaker: Kassandra
en: With the leaders dead, the resistance is over.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It'll be hard to form a resistance if they have no supplies.

speaker: Ampheres
en: Dikastes, I'm glad to see you return safely. I almost considered sending a regiment of my guard after you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That would have been overkill.

speaker: Ampheres
en: You can never be too careful when dealing with violent humans. Come, tell me, has the resistance been quashed?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I killed the leaders. With them gone their movement is dead.

speaker: Ampheres
en: A sound strategy, but i fear the problem exists at the heart of humanity itself. Another leader will rise eventually.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I know you don't trust them, but the humans will never challenge the Isu directly. You are like gods to them. You must see that.

speaker: Ampheres
en: Is is an illusion we have tried to nurture already, but it won't last. However, for now, you've done what was needed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And when a new leader rises, we will remove them as well. It's the best way to prevent you fears from happening.

speaker: Ampheres
en: Your strategy is logical, but to be ever vigilant is a daunting prospect. Perhaps it's weight someone must always carry. For now, that someone is you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I destroyed their supplies and equipment.

speaker: Ampheres
en: You believe you've saved lives by being merciful, but the truth is that more will die in the end.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I promise you - they're no threat.

speaker: Ampheres
en: You underestimate them. Yes, you've taken their means of striking now, but they will regroup and find more weapons. All you have done is delay the inevitable.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I am Dikastes. I chose the best course of action as I saw it.

speaker: Ampheres
en: Forgive my bluntness, I just believe your judgment could have been impaired by the fact you're part-human.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Apology accepted.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You must be the Hoarder?

speaker: Collector
en: The Collector!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Dust Collector, maybe. I'm here about the Minotaur.

speaker: Collector
en: The... No, no, no, I don't—I can't—I don't know anything about the Minotaur!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Ardos sent me. He says you know things.

speaker: Collector
en: Ardos! The boy. Never talk to the boy. We all promised.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm not here to break bones. I'm here for information. Give it to me and I'll be on my way.

speaker: Collector
en: I'll answer your questions, but you won't ask the right one.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Can we not play games?

speaker: Collector
en: Fine. You're going to need Theseus's armor, which I sold to be part of a collection at the fort.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What you saw has scarred you. Those scars are starting to fade. Perhaps you'd like some fresh ones?

speaker: Collector
en: No - please - I have answers! If you aim to survive that - that beast in the labyrinth, I know what you'll need!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me your secret, "Collector."

speaker: Collector
en: The armor of Theseus himself! It's the only thing that can withstand the beast. But it's not here, it's in the fort. I had to sell it!

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's nothing wrong with my armor.

speaker: Collector
en: Nikios thought his armor was the finest in the Greek world. He could have worn Theseus' when we found it, but I was the perfect fit. Minotaur struck me right in the chest... Should have died. But Nikios...? Don't make Nikios' mistake: Wear Theseus' armor.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What do you know of the boy?

speaker: Collector
en: Son of Nikios. Stubborn. A little shit. His father's son.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You remember him fondly enough, yet you refuse to speak to him.

speaker: Collector
en: If I speak, he might not listen. The truth is armor against little, misthios.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You said you sold Theseus' armor. Who has it?

speaker: Collector
en: A military commander, stationed in the fort. He has a cave filled with all sorts of prizes. The armor is his crown jewel.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sounds like a hard thing to part with.

speaker: Collector
en: No. Easy. That armor... it would have saved Nikios. It would have saved the boy's father. Yet I wore it. I didn't deserve... The armor haunted me. No point keeping ghosts in my collection.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Breathe Collector, I've learned enough. If Theseus' armor is still in the fort, I'll find it.

speaker: Collector
en: There are more pieces of Theseus' armor, I've only managed to attain two of them. But someone stole one from me! If you find it, you can have it, but give whoever took it a piece of my mind. And perhaps a piece of your blade.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The hidden cave.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Theseus' armor. It is real. I wonder how many more pieces of Theseus' armor are there...

speaker: Kassandra
en: You left a note on the board. What's happened?

speaker: Woman
en: Look at this votive figure I found at the market. It's simple, but beautiful. I have not seen its style before.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Is it valuable?

speaker: Woman
en: Not in drachmae, no. But I'm sure the priestess at the temple would appreciate it. So would the Followers of Ares, but they and their dark shrine scare me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So you'd like me to wipe out the Followers of Ares.

speaker: Woman
en: You understand quickly. I need every last one to die.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And you'll pay me to deliver it to her.

speaker: Woman
en: No, all the Followers must die.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm in.

speaker: Woman
en: Please be careful.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Chaire.

speaker: Woman
en: You're back. Have you killed them?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I took care of them. Every last one.

speaker: Woman
en: The gods favored me the day we met. Take this for your trouble, misthios.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Thank you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And you'll pay me to deliver it to her.

speaker: Woman
en: You understand quickly.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You can count on me.

speaker: Woman
en: Exactly. It must arrive without a scratch.

speaker: Kassandra
en: May the Fates be on your side.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Someone thought you might need this.

speaker: Woman
en: Thanks! Here, for your efforts, mercenary.

speaker: Steward
en: Sails need repair. Three broken oars on the top level. Two on the second level. Cracked spar. Never a day's rest, by Zeus...

speaker: Steward
en: What do you need?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Is this a bad time?

speaker: Steward
en: Every time's a bad time. There's too much work and not enough people to do it. But I'm the only person who cares about that. Wait. Did Xenia sent you?

speaker: Kassandra
en: She said you'd have work for me.

speaker: Steward
en: Well thank Poseidon. Finally! Someone competent to help! Ships are pushing into our territory and test us. Xenia wants to send a message to make sure people understand who owns this little part of the Aegean.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What kind of message do you want to send?

speaker: Steward
en: Sinking some ships while flying her colors should do the trick.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's one way to do it.

speaker: Steward
en: We're still pirates. We've got a reputation to uphold in these waters, and nothing says, "respect me" like a bit of blood spilling.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sounds to me like you're weakening the competition. Keos not big enough for your ambitions?

speaker: Steward
en: If we were going to take more territory we wouldn't be hiring the likes of you. We'd do it ourselves. Best way to prevent an attack is to strike first.

speaker: Kassandra
en: No arguments here.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll sink the ships for you. What am I targeting?

speaker: Steward
en: Destroy a few ships from Sparta, a few from Athens, and a few bandit ones, too.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's a lot of ship sinking.

speaker: Steward
en: Just make sure you're flying Xenia's colors when you do the sinking. I'll pay you well to ensure the message is understood.

speaker: Steward
en: Yes?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Oh...I'll be back once I've destroyed all the ships.

speaker: Steward
en: No need to keep me updated. Just come back when you've done the job.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've sunk the ships.

speaker: Steward
en: I knew I liked you. Xenia will be pleased that her waters are back under her control.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Flattery is fine, but I'm here for the bounty.

speaker: Steward
en: Of course.

speaker: Steward
en: Thanks for taking care of those ships, misthios.

en: Can you fucking believe it?

en: Thought she'd know better by now.

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Well, you know why. Shame though, all that cargo out there on the ocean...

speaker: Civilian 2
en: More like under, knowing Gotarzes!

speaker: Civilian 1
en: I mean how hard is it to take a merchant ship and get to Thera and back?!

speaker: Civilian 2
en: Still, Xenia could've used that miltos. The drachmae would have been helpful in her fight against...

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Something we can help you with?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Yeah, you were talking about a shipment.

speaker: Civilian 2
en: We weren't saying nothing... Nothing that concerns you, anyway.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You were, and I want to know more.

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Yeah, don't really care what you want.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Apologies, I... I've been at sea, and my curiosity got the better of me.

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Huh, no worry about manners here. Cause trouble, though, and you'll answer to Xenia.

speaker: Civilian 2
en: Yeah, we've both been to sea. Boring as fuck, and no one minded their manners on any of the vessels I sailed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'd like to find this ship.

speaker: Civilian 2
en: Well, I'll help you if you can. Then you can bring us a story.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What's miltos, anyway?

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Miltos, the next best thing to gold.

speaker: Civilian 2
en: Fucking Athenians want it all for themselves, self-important malákas.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Do you know where I can find the ship?

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Could be anywhere, knowing Gotarzes!

speaker: Civilian 2
en: I heard the plan was to intercept the shipment near Lestris island, due south of Keos.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Who's this captain you keep mentioning?

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Gotarzes, be thankful you don't know.

speaker: Civilian 2
en: The Parthenon's got more chance of staying afloat than him!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Thank you.

en: If you find that miltos, be sure to come back and share the wealth!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Of course, my friends!

en: Malákes.

en: If I can find this shipment of miltos... It's easy money.

en: There's a shipwreck, and there's the miltos.

en: Sounds like a tale for another day. I'll be seeing you.

en: Not if we see you first!

en: Ha, good one!

en: You again. Thought you'd be sick of ports, or are you looking for work?

en: Just wanted to ask about that shipment.

speaker: Civilian 2
en: Oh yeah?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You'd better tell me about that miltos shipment.

en: Don't have to tell you shit.

speaker: Civilian 2
en: Don't even try it. We're under Xenia's protection here, like everyone else.

speaker: Civilian 1
en: Go on, get out of here.

en: Told you, nothing more to say.

en: You want that shipment? Lot of water between here and Thera, better get to it.

speaker: Herodotos
en: I used to know this island as well as my own home.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Seems like a nice place to grow up.

speaker: Herodotos
en: It was. I spent a lot of time on my own or with Theodoros and Mestor. My parents are... were influential here, so they were often busy.

speaker: Kassandra
en: But it wasn't the life for you.

speaker: Herodotos
en: There's only so many ships you can see sail away as a boy before you feel the pull to leave as well.

speaker: Herodotos
en: That must be the spot Theodoros was talking about. My parents used to love walking here...

speaker: Herodotos
en: I can't believe this is where my parents last stood. Where fate decided to take them from us. I'd thought I'd write about their history on Samos and all they did one day... but not this soon.

speaker: Herodotos
en: I should have been here. Should have never left.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's no point thinking about things you "should" have done. That doesn't help.

speaker: Herodotos
en: But

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're not a fighter, Herodotos. You couldn't have stopped this.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's nothing you could have done.

speaker: Herodotos
en: But if I had tried, maybe

speaker: Kassandra
en: Maybe you would have died alongside them. And that would have helped nobody.

speaker: Herodotos
en: Perhaps you're right.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I want you to remember that while we're on Samos.

speaker: Herodotos
en: I'll try. I just wish I could have seen them once more.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Do you have a favorite memory of them?

speaker: Herodotos
en: I remember when my father taught me to swim. He tossed me off the side of the dock. I thought I was going to drown, but then I saw what I thought was a shark. I flailed my arms and kicked my legs until I made it to shore, only to see it was Theodoros with a bit of rock above his head. I still remember the sound of my father's laugh and the warmth of my mother's embrace.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Did you parents like it on Samos?

speaker: Herodotos
en: It was more than just a home to them. I saw how happy this place made them and only wanted to feel the same somewhere as well.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What did your parents think of your writing?

speaker: Herodotos
en: They always encouraged it. It helped that Theodoros was talented as well, although he always felt more drawn to poetry. If it weren't for their support, there's a good chance I would have never pursued it

speaker: Kassandra
en: If there's anything you'd like to say about your parents, you should.

speaker: Herodotos
en: I always feel more comfortable writing than I do speaking.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm not going to judge. And I know they wouldn't either.

speaker: Herodotos
en: They meant everything to me. They always encouraged me. I knew they'd be happy for me no matter what.

speaker: Herodotos
en: I'm sorry I didn't come back sooner. There was so much I wanted to tell you. To show you. Mother. you were one of the strongest people I knew. You pushed for truth no matter the obstacle. Father, your compassion is something I won't soon forget. You taught me it was OK to feel. For myself and for others. Your names and deeds won't be forgotten.

speaker: Herodotos
en: We should head back.

speaker: Herodotos
en: Watch out!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Stay close!

speaker: Herodotos
en: Those were Followers of Ares. We should see if Theodoros or Mestor know anything.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Why do I have a feeling they don't belong here?

speaker: Herodotos
en: I've never heard of them being on Samos. Something is going on. Maybe Theodoros will know. Followers of Ares here... I don't understand.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The question is whether they came on their own, or someone sent them.

speaker: Herodotos
en: Neither outcome is favorable for us... Nor Samos. I wonder what my parents would do.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Exactly what we're going to do. Protect Samos.

speaker: Theodoros
en: We can't wait much longer, do you understand?

speaker: Mestor
en: Of course. We want the same thing.

speaker: Theodoros
en: This war has caused enough problems. Samos doesn't deserve to be caught in the middle.

speaker: Mestor
en: I couldn't agree more.

speaker: Theodoros
en: You're back... I hoped you had set sail already.

speaker: Herodotos
en: Now isn't the time. We were just attacked.

speaker: Theodoros
en: Gods curse these warring Greeks. Was it the Athenians or the Spartans this time?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Neither. It was a group called the Followers of Ares.

speaker: Mestor
en: Whoever it was, thank the gods you're OK.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Have either of you heard of the Followers of Ares?

speaker: Theodoros
en: Only in name.

speaker: Mestor
en: Who are they?

speaker: Herodotos
en: They only care for one thing.. war.

speaker: Mestor
en: And you believe they're here on Samos?

speaker: Kassandra
en: They're the ones who attacked us.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Have you noticed anything suspicious lately? Strange ships docking? Groups of people you haven't seen before?

speaker: Theodoros
en: No, things have been normal. It's been a welcome change.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Something is happening here on Samos. We need answers.

speaker: Herodotos
en: She's right. If the Followers of Ares are here, there's a reason for it.

speaker: Theodoros
en: Then it's another reason for you to go. We'll handle whatever is happening here.

speaker: Herodotos
en: This is my home, too. I'm not leaving until I get to the bottom of this.

speaker: Mestor
en: If it's not safe, you shouldn't stay.

speaker: Kassandra
en: He's plenty safe with me.

speaker: Mestor
en: Of course.

speaker: Theodoros
en: Come, Mestor, if this fool won't heed our warnings, it's not our concern.

speaker: Kassandra
en: They weren't much help.

speaker: Herodotos
en: Something doesn't add up. How could Theodoros and Mestor both know nothing?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I think they were keeping something from us.

speaker: Herodotos
en: But why?

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's what we need to find out. What's next?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Forget your brothers. We should be focusing on the Followers of Ares.

speaker: Herodotos
en: You're right.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then what's our next step?

speaker: Herodotos
en: If they're somewhere on this island, they'd stay away from the city. There was a cave I used to play in as a child. It may be worth looking into.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Let's start there.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Amorges is dealt with, and I have his blade. But it's useless... Broken, and the metal is strange. I should find a blacksmith.

speaker: Broken Blade of the Ancients
en: Amorges's personal weapon, this blade was shattered after a fierce battle with the Eagle Bearer.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The Oikos of the Olympians has a blacksmith known for his skill in working rare metals. I should take the sword there.

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: Kopis or '—what do you need?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Have you seen anything like this before?

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: Zeus' balls! Do you know what this is?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Broken?

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: It's adamantine! This stuff is priceless! And I don't mind telling you I'm the one man in the islands who knows how to properly work it. I'll need more adamantine to fix it, though. A lot more.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Will this help? The metal looks similar.

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: What the—where in Hades are you getting this stuff? No, I don't want to know.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Is this enough to repair the sword?

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: I wish I could say yes, but then I'd be lying... Bring me more, and I'll make you a sword fit for a god.

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: You're back! You got it, didn't you? I can smell Adamantine, and you smell good!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Here. Don't tell me you need more, because I've run out of necks to cut it from.

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: There's real passion behind your words, I can feel it. I'm personally glad to say that these will do. The blood on them is a nice touch, by the way. Helps with the quenching.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I do what I can.

speaker: Artisan Smith
en: Wait here. This won't take long.
