en: I do your dirty work, and you don't pay me? It's personal.

speaker: Obelia
en: Look on the bright side—I'm allowing you to walk away with your life.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Here's your treasure. I hope it's cursed.

speaker: Obelia
en: I could tell you were a smart one.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Satisfied?

speaker: Obelia
en: Yes. Now get off my fucking ship.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There was no treasure.

speaker: Obelia
en: Then why are you here?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I came to tell you there's nothing there. Someone else must have got there first.

speaker: Obelia
en: Then I'll kill you and check your remains, just to be sure.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Deal's off. Now I'll kill you for wasting my time.

speaker: Obelia
en: You haven't got a chance. Take her out!

speaker: Weakening the Enemy
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Weeding Out Athenian Forces
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Poseidon
en: That's enough!

speaker: Hades
en: No need to shout. This isn't your domain, brother.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Hades has nothing left to offer you. You were never meant to stay here. Nor Elysium. You didn't belong on Kephallonia, and you didn't belong in Sparta. I can offer you a place you do belong. It's time you finally found it. Atlantis awaits.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Anywhere's better than here.

speaker: Hades
en: I won't forget this.

speaker: Hades
en: No!

speaker: Poseidon
en: There's no need for that here. You're safe.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've heard that before.

speaker: Poseidon
en: This place isn't like any other you've been. There's no Persephone. No Hades.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Just you.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Just me, Dikastes Basileus, the Grand Adjudicator of all Atlantis.

speaker: Poseidon
en: But to you, I am Poseidon. What I'm offering you, Keeper of the Staff, is a place at my side. Join me as my Dikastes.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Welcome home.

speaker: Kassandra
en: This place is... the real Atlantis. I mean—it's intact. I thought this city was destroyed.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Every seven years, our great city begins a new cycle—if judged to be imperfect.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And who's the judge?

speaker: Poseidon
en: Before your arrival, it was my decision alone. Now that I have you at my side, I intend for this cycle to last an eternity.

speaker: Kassandra
en: If you're the Dikastes Basileus, you expect me to be...

speaker: Poseidon
en: Dikastes—the judge. Be my hand. Be my hand in laying and enforcing judgement in Atlantis.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Well, I must warn you that I'm not always right.

speaker: Poseidon
en: I was both surprised and encouraged by your actions in the underworld. Fortunes were exchanged in response to your choices. But trust that I learned your reverence to justice is true.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Hades must have told you about my Staff.

speaker: Poseidon
en: He didn't have to. As is the way with all heroes, your journey has become the stuff of Atlantean legend.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then you know my Staff is the reason I'm here. I need to learn how to master it.

speaker: Poseidon
en: This land is a paradise of power for those with Isu devices. But all in good time.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So you expect me to live among you. A home among gods?

speaker: Poseidon
en: Gods?! We're much more than the human conception of gods. Your father called us The Ones Who Came Before, but as Aletheia told you, we are the Isu.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You know about my Staff, Pythagoras, and Aletheia? I'm starting to feel very watched.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Your trials in both Elysium and the underworld—no, your triumphs there—are known to us.

speaker: Kassandra
en: My "trials" forced me into a rebellion. They made me face the dead. My hardships make me a good Dikastes?

speaker: Poseidon
en: We don't always choose our path, but in this case, your blood chose for you. You possess both DNA strands—the best of humans and Isu. I have no doubt that you are our mutual future.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's an honor. Where do I start?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Call yourself whatever you want. You people have used me, lied to me, and tried to kill me.

speaker: Poseidon
en: You've done the same to others when it was necessary. But it's all the more reason to overcome that now. Lead by example. My people can change, just as you can.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm listening.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I cry. I bleed. I make as many mistakes as anyone. How can I be the one you're looking for?

speaker: Poseidon
en: It is precisely for those reasons that I know to trust you. Your sense of awareness is essential.

speaker: Kassandra
en: If you say so.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Humans have five sense to understand the world around them. We have been blessed a sixth—knowledge.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Ah, no, it is not merely your Vision of the Eagle. The essence of that sense sleeps now, but it can be awoken in Atlantis. Your Staff is more than a key. It's a bridge between who you are now, and who you must become.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And if I fully awaken this sixth sense, I'll have mastered the Staff?

speaker: Poseidon
en: That, and more. Come, let me show you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I accessed power sources in Elysium and the underworld. They helped my "knowledge," I think, but they haven't changed my senses.

speaker: Poseidon
en: In Atlantis, you'll find the sources that awaken your new sense much more concentrated. Not only will your knowledge grow here, but it will thrive. You'll find three such sources once you leave this palace. You know them as Keeper's Insights.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Doesn't look like anyone can get through.

speaker: Poseidon
en: It's blocked to those who haven't full access to our knowledge. Find the source of that knowledge within this palace. Try to pass through once you do.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's strange, but it feels like the Staff is becoming a part of me. I think I'm starting to understand. It's like I can feel Isu memories and hear their wisdom.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Now I know what you meant about the sources being more concentrated. I feel different.

speaker: Poseidon
en: Many things are different here, Dikastes. You'll discover that in time. Atlantis awaits you. I have one rule that is absolute. Our technology cannot be used on my human civilians. Their bodies cannot withstand the power. The Isu know this above all.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So, I'm free to go? What task should the Dikastes do first?

speaker: Poseidon
en: Even Atlantis is not a perfect society—it yearns for balance. So, be that balance. Then, when your role as guide to the people is fulfilled, it may well be perfection. Don't worry. You've already earned my respect, which is a trial in itself.

speaker: Atlantean Messenger
en: Dikastes, his eminence, Atlas, humbly requests that you join him at his Doma to discuss a matter of grave importance.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Right... I'll make sure to stop by.

speaker: Kassandra
en: "His eminence"? This place has more kings than Sparta.

speaker: Herodotos
en: When you're ready, meet me at the Pnyx in Athens.

speaker: Perikles
en: The Spartans may draw near to our walls, but we must come together now for the glory of Athens.

speaker: Civilian
en: Glory for you!

speaker: Kleon
en: Friends! Friends, please! Just because the Spartans are near our walls does not mean we can act like them.

speaker: Kleon
en: A good crop! Shame the Spartans burned the fields where it grew. The Parthenon is glorious, Perikles, but at what cost? How many triremes could we have built instead?

speaker: Perikles
en: We must not become divided

speaker: Kleon
en: We are divided, and the Spartans are winning! Act, Perikles, or I will!

speaker: Herodotos
en: Oh good, you came. Things are worse than I feared. Kleon has turned the mob. We have to hurry.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Where?

speaker: Herodotos
en: To Perikles. There's much to do. And many unknowns on our horizon.

speaker: Athenian Soldier
en: Stay back.

speaker: Herodotos
en: She's no threat to Perikles, I assure you.

speaker: Perikles
en: Ah, Herodotos. It's fine. Let them through.

speaker: Herodotos
en: It's good to see you again, Perikles.

speaker: Perikles
en: And you as well. I only wish it were under better circumstances. And who's this?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Kassandra.

speaker: Perikles
en: Welcome, Kassandra. And what did you think of your first taste of Athens?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I think you and Kleon both made good points.

speaker: Perikles
en: Good points aren't at all what the crowd seemed to care about. They're afraid, and Kleon indulged their fear.

speaker: Perikles
en: Nothing to say? Others would do well to realize silence is as much as an answer as anything else. A crowd would seize the first easy answer that comes its way, like a hungry dog on a bone.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I think you did a great job.

speaker: Perikles
en: It's so easy to forget the good someone has done when times become hard.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Perikles, we've come to

speaker: Herodotos
en: We must choose our moment wisely and speak our words more privately.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Fine. We've come to you on... urgent business.

speaker: Perikles
en: As does everybody.

speaker: Herodotos
en: I may have told Kassandra you'd invite her to your symposium.

speaker: Perikles
en: You'd ask me to exclude every Athenian and invite an outsider instead? You heard the crowd. They don't need another reason to hate me.

speaker: Herodotos
en: If she's working for you, maybe the prying eyes will see her as a servant.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm no one's "servant."

speaker: Herodotos
en: Kassandra, this is Athens. If you want something, sometimes you have to play the role.

speaker: Perikles
en: And what exactly is it that you want?

speaker: Kassandra
en: We're all after something, even you.

speaker: Perikles
en: You're better at reading others than you let on.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm looking for a woman who's very important to me. Herodotos said a symposium could be useful for gaining information.

speaker: Perikles
en: He would be correct. I can get you in, although I can't promise the information you seek will be found.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Just tell me what to do.

speaker: Perikles
en: First, check on my colleague, Metiochos. He was meant to meet me today, and it's not like him to miss an appointment.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Done.

speaker: Perikles
en: My friend, Phidias, needs to be taken out of Athens as soon as possible.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Anything else?

speaker: Perikles
en: Yes, there's an ostracism vote taking place that could use your... influence.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Metiochos... you said he was your colleague?

speaker: Perikles
en: A politician and ally. He's one of my most loyal friends.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Phidias... the famous sculptor? What did he do, exactly?

speaker: Perikles
en: He stands accused of multiple offenses and is awaiting trial. You'll find him under close guard at his workshop.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Ostracism?

speaker: Herodotos
en: Exile is a term you may be more familiar with. Here in Athens, we vote between two people to decide who should leave.

speaker: Perikles
en: It's between the , Anaxagoras, and another man. On trial for impiety. My contact near the agora will give you the details.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll do it.

speaker: Perikles
en: I'll expect you to use discretion.

speaker: Herodotos
en: That went well! It isn't exactly an invitation, but the promise is just as good. Although I'm sure he'll still ask Aspasia if it's OK.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So long as it comes.

speaker: Hermes
en: No one stands up to Persephone's guards. Let alone best them in battle.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me your name or you're next.

speaker: Hermes
en: Ah! I'm Hermes. As you're holding my proudest creation, that means you're a descendant of Pythagoras. I know just why you're here. You need to harness its power. Now, your name.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The Staff calls me Keeper, but you can call me Kassandra. What is this place?

speaker: Hermes
en: Keeper! A great name, with a great journey ahead of you. This is the paradise of Elysium, presided over by the mighty Persephone herself. Elysium was a gift from her husband Hades. This beautiful realm she crafted in her image is the only joy she gets from the underworld—she's his prisoner. But, she's come into her role as queen with much aplomb!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Elysium—resting place of heroes. When I was a girl, I'd dream of seeing it with my own eyes. Then why would Persephone attack me?

speaker: Hermes
en: Most rulers don't take the sudden invasion of a lone outsider lightly. Speaking of which, the appearance of a living human is quite unexpected.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm supposed to go through trials, and eventually leave this place. There was a Great Seal, and the Staff talks... It's all very complicated.

speaker: Hermes
en: Allow me to explain. The Staff is a gift, not a toy! It can be a key, a weapon, and a way to attain power until the very end of time. Here, you'll find the means to control it before it controls you. After that... There is a gate that leads out of Elysium, but the only way to it is through Persephone, and she'd never allow that.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I need to get to that gate.

speaker: Hermes
en: Try talking to her. Who knows? Maybe she'll convince you to stay. Or, you could find Hekate, Persephone's top advisor and closest friend. Or... you could prove yourself.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Prove myself how?

speaker: Hermes
en: Persephone sent guards because she's concerned. There are reports of lawlessness in Deukalion's Heritage south of here.

speaker: Hermes
en: Why am I telling you all this? You said it yourself—it's very complicated. Elysium may look like paradise, but we all have our secrets.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm thinking I go straight to Persephone.

speaker: Hermes
en: Not so fast! Give her some time to cool down. When you introduce yourself, you'll find her in her majestic akropolis, perched high above the Asphodel Fields.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I could talk to Hekate.

speaker: Hermes
en: You could, though she prefers to keep to herself. The dwellers of Pheraia's Retreat, which is to the east, might know of her whereabouts. I'd ask them.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Maybe I should investigate Deukalion's Heritage.

speaker: Hermes
en: Persephone responds best to action. We need to smother them immediately if there's a whiff of trouble against her.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me about yourself.

speaker: Hermes
en: Me? Well, I've never had anyone ask me before. I work west of here. It's a modest workshop, but all great things appear modest at first, don't they?

speaker: Kassandra
en: What can you tell me about my Staff? I need to learn how to use it.

speaker: Hermes
en: Find my energy sources—the Perceptions of Hermes—across Elysium to imbue both you and the Staff with power. Only then are you ready to move onward. You can't wield the Staff without them! Are you certain there's nothing else you'd like to know?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Chaire.

speaker: Hermes
en: When you've sorted your affairs with Persephone, come see me in Minos' Faith. I look forward to hearing about your progress.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I will.

speaker: Hermes
en: I almost forgot. I've invented just the thing for you flightless humans in Elysium—the Wings of Hermes. Go, enjoy them!

speaker: Kassandra
en: And you must be... the "warriors."

speaker: Ankos
en: Look, brother—the final member of our Minotaur-hunting party has arrived! When the beast sees our assembled might, he will moo miserably in fear! ...Do Minotaurs moo, or... ?

speaker: Araxis
en: If it's all right with both of you, I'd like to strike the killing blow. Or, can we at least say I struck the killing blow? ...I'm willing to haggle down to "played a key role in distracting the Minotaur while allowing the killing blow to be struck."

speaker: Kassandra
en: The Minotaur is a mythical creature—only someone just as mythical could slay it.

speaker: Araxis
en: ...You're talking about me, right?

speaker: Ankos
en: The only "myths" about you, little brother, are the ones pater paid to keep quiet.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The killing blow will go to the warrior with the greatest skill and courage in battle.

speaker: Araxis
en: Then I shall wear the Minotaur's entrails as my necklace!

speaker: Kassandra
en: This can only end well.

speaker: Araxis
en: Are you ready to ride?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Let's slay a Minotaur.

speaker: Araxis
en: Leiandros says it lives in the Cave of the Brave, on the Dikte Plateau. I say let the Mino-tournament BEGIN!

speaker: Araxis
en: ...If the Minotaur eats humans and lives right next to the population of Pephka, how are they all still alive?

speaker: Ankos
en: Perhaps the diet of Pephkans disagrees with him?

speaker: Araxis
en: Good thinking, brother! Let us dip our blades in rich oils and onions to gain an edge in combat!

speaker: Ankos
en: Behold, brother; the home of the Minotaur!

speaker: Araxis
en: Isn't he supposed to live in a labyrinth?

speaker: Ankos
en: That's a myth.

speaker: Araxis
en: Isn't the Minotaur a myth?

speaker: Ankos
en: No, he's the half-bull, half-human bastard son of King Minos' wife.

speaker: Araxis
en: ...Sounds like a myth to me.

speaker: Araxis
en: I hear the Minotaur was slain by Theseus.

speaker: Ankos
en: Impossible! If Theseus killed the Minotaur, how can it be here?

speaker: Ankos
en: BEWARE BEAST! For soon I shall use your spinal column as as an eating utensil!

speaker: Araxis
en: Don't warn him.

speaker: Unknown
en: ROOOOOOOOAR!!!

speaker: Ankos
en: Is that him, brother?! He sounds large! I thought he was a mini-taur... Perhaps we should courageously flee?

speaker: Araxis
en: No, no, brother—onwards, into the dark!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Ominous. Must be in the right place.

speaker: Ankos
en: There's no glory here... only death.

speaker: Unknown
en: ROOOOOOOOAR!!!

speaker: Ankos
en: No-no-no! I only ever wanted to be a baker!

speaker: Araxis
en: Brother! Wait! There's more glory in beast-slaying than in bread-making!

speaker: Unknown
en: ROOOOOOOOAR!!!

speaker: Araxis
en: Uh, I should check on my brother. The baking business is fierce, you know! Good luuuuuuck!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Pephka, home of heroes.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Whatever lives down here must be a monster.

speaker: Kassandra
en: These bodies haven't been torn apart by a Minotaur, they've been... arranged? These bodies have arrow wounds and cuts from weapons too small to be wielded by a Minotaur.

speaker: Unknown
en: ROOOOOOOOOAR...!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Did the Minotaur just... cough?

speaker: Unknown
en: This is your last chance to flee, mortal!

speaker: Unknown
en: I. Am... The Minotaur! Roooooooar!!!

speaker: Kassandra
en: ...What?

speaker: Unknown
en: Drop all your valuables and flee in terror, mortal! L-leave me your drachmae and you shall be spared! otherwise, DEATH BY HOOF AWAITS YOU!

speaker: Unknown
en: FEAR MY MOO!!! ...Fear it?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Maláka... I'm going to start stabbing until someone tells me what's going on!

speaker: Unknown
en: Don't kill me, don't kill me, don't kill me! They made me do it! Their masks are even scarier than mine! It's worth it... it's worth it... I-I'm not a bad man...

speaker: Kassandra
en: The last Minotaur I killed talked less.

speaker: Unknown
en: Killed?! No, uh—we don't have to use the "K" word! I mean, grrr!

speaker: Unknown
en: Please, no—they made me! Don't kill me!

speaker: Unknown
en: ...Grr! I said GRRR!!! Oh, fuck it. Hi.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's no need for more blood. Just keep your horns away from me, and tell me what's going on here. You can take off that mask.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me what's going on, or I'll cut it out of you. And take off that malákas mask.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Leiandros?!

speaker: Leiandros
en: I told you nothing is what it seems in Pephka! I'm happy to refund any expenses incurred

speaker: Leiandros
en: Please, it's my daughter, Amara! Masked men are holding her captive deep in the canyons of Dikte Plateau.

speaker: Kassandra
en: "Masked men." What kind of masks?

speaker: Leiandros
en: Uh, uh—white like marble, bleeding from their eyes. Horrific.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The Cult.

speaker: Leiandros
en: They control everything in Pephka... lure champions from all over with the promise of Minotaur-slaying glory, only to swindle and ambush them down here in the dark. Honorless. If I don't do as they say, Amara dies. If I take off my mask, or tell my wife, or ask for help... she dies.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me about your daughter.

speaker: Leiandros
en: Amara... the sound of her laughter is sunlight on my skin. She is joy, misthios. ...One night the Masked Men took that joy from me. They needed my silver tongue to lure wealthy warriors to their Trials. In Amara, they found all they needed to control me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You said the Cult—the "masked men" have your daughter in the canyons of Dikte Plateau— There are a lot of canyons.

speaker: Leiandros
en: But only one holds Amara. There's a place called Zakros—an ancient ruin, and a bastion of the masked men's power. I go there every night, hoping to catch a glimpse of her. But I never have. I fear they keep her underground, where she'll never see the sun.

speaker: Kassandra
en: How many men have you sent to their deaths with a speech and a smile?

speaker: Leiandros
en: Thousands. More. But their lives will never outweigh my Amara. She's all I have... but now I have you, don't I? You... you can free her from those malákes masked men!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Tell me, whose face would Amara wish to see rescue her? Mine? ...Or her father's? Be brave, Leiandros.

speaker: Leiandros
en: Bravery. Yes. You're right, misthios. No matter what, I must be there for my Amara. Please, will you join me?

speaker: Kassandra
en: She's your daughter. You must save her!

speaker: Leiandros
en: But they'd cut me down! You think she would want to see her father die?!

speaker: Kassandra
en: She would want her father to protect her!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Coward.

speaker: Leiandros
en: You're right. I'm a coward. And a man cannot be any more than he is. That's enough for me, but... it's not enough to save Amara. For that, I'll need your help.

speaker: Kassandra
en: We will save your daughter... together.

speaker: Leiandros
en: Thank you, misthios. Meet me outside the ruins of Zakros on Dikte Plateau. That's where my daughter is, and where I must be.

speaker: Ankos
en: Nothing to see here! Just a couple of brave warriors, bravely being brave. Move along!

speaker: Araxis
en: So when did you run away? Thirty seconds after us, or twenty?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I don't run.

speaker: Araxis
en: Right! Neither do we!

speaker: When the Weak Fall
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Where Feathers Fall
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Myrrine
en: My lamb! You've been gone so long.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Brasidas is dead.

speaker: Myrrine
en: No.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Deimos killed him in battle.

speaker: Myrrine
en: And what of my son?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Kleon shot him in the back with an arrow. He fell. I don't think he survived.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Kleon fired an arrow into Deimos' back. The wound didn't look fatal—he could still be alive.

speaker: Myrrine
en: Malákas Kleon! I'll kill him with my bare hands.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's done, mater. I already sent that snake to the Styx.

speaker: Myrrine
en: My family...

speaker: Myrrine
en: You're all I have left.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Mater, there's something I need to do.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I need to go to Mount Taygetos, where it all began.

speaker: Kassandra
en: My whole life's been spent fighting and running. Running from my past, fighting to forget. I can't do this anymore.

speaker: Myrrine
en: My heart was shattered on that mountain.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I need to put that night behind me, once and for all.

speaker: Myrrine
en: I'm coming with you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: This is where everything changed. It's like I never left.

speaker: Myrrine
en: Alexios!

speaker: Deimos
en: On the edge of the world, a mother calls out to her child. Touching.

speaker: Myrrine
en: Alexios, please.

speaker: Deimos
en: You use that name as if it means something to me.

speaker: Myrrine
en: It's the name your father and I gave you.

speaker: Deimos
en: Was that before, or after, you brought me to this mountain to die?

speaker: Myrrine
en: It was the Cult. I tried to save you. I did everything! The priests told me you were dead.

speaker: Deimos
en: And they told me you abandoned your son!

speaker: Myrrine
en: Alexios, come to me. We are your family. We can go home.

speaker: Deimos
en: Family? Home?

speaker: Deimos
en: My sword is my family. The battlefield is my home.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I promised to bring him back, mater. But the Cult has poisoned his mind.

speaker: Deimos
en: Promised to bring me back to mater did you? You didn't bring me here. Why don't you tell our mater the truth?

speaker: Kassandra

en: No. I'm certain it's Leda's. It must be.

en: Right as always, old friend. Which means we're one step closer to finding Leda, I think.

speaker: Barnabas
en: You think correctly! The gods would never lie. Aside from Dolos. And Apate. But never mind them.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Chaire, priestess. Anything I can help you with?

speaker: Priestess
en: That Spartan leader is finally dead. But those malákes soldiers who follow him... some of them still plague our land and sea. I want them all gone.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So you want me to kill all the Spartans?

speaker: Priestess
en: Not strong enough. I want all their ships destroyed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll handle this.

speaker: Priestess
en: You'll be doing divine work.

speaker: Kassandra
en: May the Fates be on your side.

speaker: Priestess
en: Back already? Did you destroy them all?

speaker: Kassandra
en: It would be hard to piece them back together.

speaker: Priestess
en: I knew the Gods intended us to meet. Please, take this.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Thank you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What... what was in that box? My body is tingling like mad. There must be more of these somewhere.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Is there something you need?

speaker: Man
en: I've got excess mandrake among my wares, and there's a witch nearby willing to pay a good price for it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sounds like a good match.

speaker: Man
en: It is, but I've got a healthy fear of the wolves that prowl near her home. And a healthy fear of witches, come to think of it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You want me to bring it to her.

speaker: Man
en: I know I asked the right person.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll help you.

speaker: Man
en: The Fates are working in my favor.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Chaire, stranger.

speaker: Kassandra
en: A man told me you needed this.

speaker: Witch
en: Ah, yes. I was wondering when this would arrive. Here, your payment.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Now that you've forged my friend's name on the citizen's list, there's one more thing that needs to be done.

speaker: Kassandra
en: If you'd told me this needed to be done before, I could have taken care of it already.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Maybe, but this way I get to see you more often.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Next time you want me to do two things, tell me both at the same time.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: The second is dependent on the first. I needed to know it was complete... I didn't expect you to get so upset about it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Just tell me what you need.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Unfortunately, getting Sophanes' name on the list doesn't make him a citizen. He also needs a witness who can validate his citizenship.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So you want me to be the witness?

speaker: Alkibiades
en: If only it were that easy. No, there's someone I have in mind. An extremely handsome man by the name of Peiroos.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sophanes can wait a bit longer.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: I knew you couldn't help but come back for more.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll find your... handsome witness.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Perfect! I knew you'd be willing to help.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There must be a good reason we can't be witnesses?

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Of course. The witness must be an Athenian citizen, but it can't be a friend. Be careful with Peiroos, though. It's easy to... lose oneself in his gaze.

speaker: Kassandra
en: If there's more after this, I want to know now.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Of course! This should be the last thing.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Should?

speaker: Alkibiades
en: I mean is.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Time to find Peiroos.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: He's often around the justice building on the east side of the agora.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And I just... ask him to help?

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Peiroos needs to say that the parents of Sophanes were both Athenians. How you get him to do it is up to you.

speaker: Kassanda
en: The witness. There you are.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's the guy Alkibiades called handsome? Can't say I agree with him.

speaker: Peiroos
en: You tell Dion I'm not giving him any more. If he wants to talk to me, he can come himself.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm not here about debts.

speaker: Peiroos
en: Well, what do you want, then?

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's something I need your help with. Well, you'd actually be helping someone else.

speaker: Peiroos
en: That someone sent you tells me it's something I'd be better off avoiding.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You just need to validate a man's citizenship. Alkibiades said it's an easy role for you to play.

speaker: Kassandra
en: There's a man trying to become an Athenian citizen. You're going to be his witness.

speaker: Peiroos
en: Me? Why?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Because Alkibiades said you're the one to do it.

speaker: Peiroos
en: Alkibiades? He is persistent... And who is this man I'm meant to help?

speaker: Kassandra
en: His name is Sophanes.

speaker: Peiroos
en: Sophanes? I know that name well. I won't help you, though, not for him.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I don't know him. Why don't you want to help?

speaker: Peiroos
en: A true misthios – never get all the information up front. Sophanes betrayed his men for drachmae. He deserves death, not citizenship. Look, it isn't your fault - you didn't know. But now you do.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I don't care what he's done. You're still going to help me.

speaker: Peiroos
en: I won't help someone who betrayed his men to the enemy for drachmae – and you shouldn't want to, either. Men like him don't deserve to live, let alone be citizens like the rest of us.

speaker: Peiroos
en: Look, it isn't your fault – you didn't know. But now you do.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're going to help, but it's your choice how bloody you are when you do. Or maybe I'll go to Dion and see if he'll pay me to get what you owe him.

speaker: Peiroos
en: You can't threaten me and expect to get what you want. You'll regret that.

speaker: Peiroos
en: That's enough! I'll do what you want. Even after all Sophanes did, he gets another chance...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sounds like Dion may be sending someone to collect from you. Wouldn't it be nice to have the drachmae you need?

speaker: Peiroos
en: I... fine. I'll do what you want.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're right. If it's like you say, he doesn't deserve to call himself an Athenian.

speaker: Peiroos
en: I'm glad we can agree. I'm just sorry you had to come all this way to find out.

speaker: Peiroos
en: Make sure Sophanes doesn't know I was part of this.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: You've returned!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sokrates too, it seems.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Much like you, he just can't seem to stay away. I hope there were no issues?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Yes. He just needed a little push.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Ah. I was worried about that. Well, you did the right thing.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Peiroos didn't want to do it. When he told me why, I understood.

speaker: Alkibades
en: I see. Sophanes will be disappointed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You kept information from me – information that would have been nice to know.

speaker: Alkibades
en: I believe people like Sophanes deserve second chances. I didn't think what he did mattered to you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Next time, let me decide what matters to me.

speaker: Alkibiades
en: Understood. I should give Sophanes the news.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's done.

speaker: Alibiades
en: So it is. I'll let Sophanes know what happened.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Do not bad citizens do harm to their neighbors, and good citizens, good? Is it impossible to tell if someone will be good or bad without first giving them a chance?

speaker: Kassandra
en: A person isn't the same forever. Someone bad can become good.

speaker: Sokrates
en: But is the inverse not also true? Someone considered good can then become bad... How can we predict someone's actions now, let alone in the future?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Nobody changes – not enough, at least.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Then do a person's actions stay with them for life? If a man steals a sword from a blacksmith, is he bad until death takes him? How can we predict a person's future actions?

speaker: Kassandra
en: We can't. One thing I've learned is people are unpredictable. It's what makes my job so hard sometimes.

speaker: Sokrates
en: If what you say is true, we can either hope we are right, and that people will be good, or limit risk by not giving people like Sophanes a chance.

speaker: Kassandra
en: A person's past shows who they'll become. The one easy part of my job is how predictable people can be.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Then a war criminal such as Sophanes must bear that choice, with no hope to change how he is seen.

speaker: Sokrates
en: I wonder then if bad actions can reverse good, or good actions can reverse bad. Perhaps we can speak on that another time.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Thank the gods.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Kassandra! There you are.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Am I interrupting?

speaker: Timotheos
en: This is where I used to practice sparring with my father. After he retired to the fishing business, he lost interest. But I kept up the practice on my own.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Doesn't training on your own get lonely?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sparring without a partner isn't a real challenge.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Are you trying to goad me into a sparring match, mercenary?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I might be interested in some friendly competition.

speaker: Timotheos
en: I... don't think that's a good idea.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Are you scared, Athenian?

speaker: Timotheos
en: I just... Fine. Let's spar.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Let's see what you've got.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That all you've got?

speaker: Timotheos
en: Ha! I'm just getting started.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Come on, mercenary! Keep up!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Please! You're the one slowing down.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Filthy Spartans!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Timotheos, are you OK?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You fought well, Athenian. Timotheos?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Timotheos, what are you doing?

speaker: Timotheos
en: I—No. Stop. Stop.

speaker: Timotheos
en: No! No! Stay back! Get away from me!

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll stay back. I promise.

speaker: Timotheos
en: I—don't know what I'll do if you get too close.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm not going to hurt you. Let me

speaker: Timotheos
en: Don't you get it? I might hurt you if you don't stay away!

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're not going to hurt me, Timotheos.

speaker: Timotheos
en: You don't... you don't know that. I don't know if I could stop myself right now.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Even if you did try to hurt me, I'm more than capable of fending you off.

speaker: Timotheos
en: That's not... You're underestimating what I'll do when this happens.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I know you're stronger than whatever this is.

speaker: Timotheos
en: When I get like this... If I lose control for even a second, the terrible things I see myself doing...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Timotheos...

speaker: Timotheos
en: No, no, no. Stop. Stop!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Just breathe.

speaker: Timotheos
en: I'm OK. I'm OK. Thank you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Just calm down.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Like it's that fucking easy!

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're safe, Timotheos. I promise.

speaker: Timotheos
en: I need to be alone right now. I—I'm sorry.

speaker: Timotheos
en: I feel... better. Thank you. Would you mind... staying with me for a moment?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Whatever you need.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Father handled coming back from the war so much better than I did. Any loud noise or unexpected hand on my shoulder, and my heart bursts from my chest. But he never flinched.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Did you tell him?

speaker: Timotheos
en: I couldn't bear to tell father the reason I was discharged, let alone this. I wanted to make him proud.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Why were you discharged?

speaker: Timotheos
en: I... lost control in a battle and killed one of my comrades. My commander and I were close, so he discharged me with mania instead of charging me with treason. When I returned from the war, father never asked why. I don't know if he suspected or...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Maybe he was hiding his struggles the way you hid yours.

speaker: Timotheos
en: If that's true, he was strong enough to hide it from everyone. I'm too weak to even hide it from you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Pain doesn't make you weak. Timotheos. You're a survivor.

speaker: Timotheos
en: When the battle hasn't been won, is there really honor in coming back alive?

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's going to be all right, Timotheos.

speaker: Timotheos
en: For the first time, I think it might be.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Timotheos, you're a strong person. Anyone can see that.

speaker: Timotheos
en: You think I'm strong?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You know you're tough

speaker: Timotheos
en: Still nice to hear you say it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Maybe if you stopped brooding for a second, you'd see it, too.

speaker: Timotheos
en: My father just died.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I... You're right. Sorry

speaker: Timotheos
en: It's... fine.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Anyone who cares for people the way you do is strong, Timotheos.

speaker: Timotheos
en: You think i'm caring.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Of course. You care for Lykinos... and others.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Others?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You're going to be all right, Timotheos.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Thank you. And... under normal circumstances, I would never tell you to stay away from me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: We could get closer now.

speaker: Timotheos
en: What are we waiting for?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I think we're close enough for now.

speaker: Timotheos
en: All right. this is nice, too.

speaker: Kassandra
en: War isn't easy, Timotheos. Everyone comes back with wounds that never heal.

speaker: Timotheos
en: Physical scars fade. I'm not sure the ones I have ever will.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It's going to be all right, Timotheos.

speaker: Timotheos
en: For the first time, I think it might be.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I should check in on Timotheos and Lykinos at their father's house.

speaker: Wrath of Hephaistos
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Wrecking Athenian Forces
en: was a virtual representation of one of Kassandra's genetic memories, relived by Layla Hassan through the Portable Animus HR-8.5.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Bryce! Wait!

speaker: Bryce
en: Ligeia! LIGEIA!!!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Maláka.

speaker: Bryce
en: Ligeia! Where are you?!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Bryce! You have no idea what you're—BRYCE!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Angry snakes. A bad omen.

speaker: Kassandra
en: This looks like the way.

speaker: Bryce
en: Please, say something!

speaker: Bryce
en: Do you remember the poems we read to each other? Do you remember our promise?

speaker: Bryce
en: I'm sorry I wasn't there that night. I'm sorry I was late.

speaker: Bryce
en: Don't forgive me, just find me.

speaker: Bryce
en: I brought you a rose. Just—follow my voice. Find me... and I'll give it to you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Only one myth speaks of turning victims to stone.

speaker: Bryce
en: I—I hear you, my love! Look at me, Ligeia! Please, just look me in the eye...

speaker: Bryce
en: ...Ligeia?

speaker: Bryce
en: No!

speaker: Bryce
en: Ligeia, it's me, Bryce!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Bryce!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Ligeia must have picked up the artifact and transformed into that creature. I wonder how many people have become "The Writhing Dread" over the centuries...?

speaker: Unknown
en: ...Wield fear as a weapon, may our enemies crumble...

speaker: Kassandra
en: "Someone, I tell you, in another time will remember us."

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Greetings, young one. Come to offer Asklepios a sacrifice?

speaker: Kassandra
en: No, but I'm searching for a Spartan mother who may have.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: The great goddess Hera guides many mothers to this sacred place. Surely I'm too feeble to remember them all.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What are these stone slabs for?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: These are records. We document all who pass through—their illnesses, treatments—so that the glory of Asklepios can be celebrated.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then I don't need your memory. I just need to find the right stone.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Um, yes, of course. That's very wise, indeed. If only I had the time to help you...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Listen, I'm not here to hurt you. I'm just looking for my mater.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: It's Chrysis. She's got every priest in the sanctuary under her thumb, and she'll squash anyone who feeds information to the Eagle Bearer.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then don't tell me anything—just bring me to the stone that can.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Follow me, then. Quickly, we must be discreet.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Lead the way.

speaker: Kassandra
en: My mother came through here, and unless you want me to paint these stones with your blood, you'll tell me what you know.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Please... It's Chrysis. She said that anyone who talks to the Eagle Bearer will be paying a visit to Hades.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Then don't talk. Just bring me to the stone that can.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Follow me, then. Quickly, we must be discreet.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Lead the way.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: This way. Over here. If anyone is watching, they'll have my head.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What kind of sanctuary isn't safe for its priests?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Times have changed, Eagle Bearer.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Ah! I remember this tale. Written during the time of the great Helot Revolt. You would have been only a child.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I don't need the history, just the details.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: It tells the tale of a woman with worms in her throat. Asklepios took off her head so we could remove them, then reattached it in her sleep.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Definitely not the right one. I wonder what Hippokrates would think of these... treatments.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Hippokrates is a fine healer. Showed so much promise.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Showed? He's healing the sick right now.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: He puts too much faith in his hands, and not enough in the gods.

speaker: Kassandra
en: When it comes to life and death, I prefer hands. Are all the testimonies so... outrageous?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Writers today—Thucydides, Euripides, the petulant Aristophanes... All of them try for realism, but—what really inspires is greatness, magic, gods!

speaker: Timoxenos
en: This one tells the tale of a man with sword wounds. A pack of dogs licked him clean, and eureka! A man's best friend indeed.

speaker: Kassandra
en: This is hopeless.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: These stories give people hope, Eagle Bearer.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Well, I'm losing mine. Tell me about Chrysis.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: A very powerful, dangerous woman. But it was not always so. She was abandoned here as a child and taken in by the priests. Taught the ways of the gods. She learned very quickly, was very strong-willed, and before too long it was the priests who listened to her. She was loved. But there's an anger in her heart that could not be soothed. So when her methods turned to madness, anyone who opposed her got...

speaker: Kassandra
en: Got what?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: I've already said too much.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And what about this one? Let me guess: it tells the tale of a blind woman who had her eyes licked by snakes.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: It reads "Of Sparta. Came here with child. Sought pity from the gods."

speaker: Kassandra
en: Why is most of it scratched out?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Oh, I um... I'll just tell you. I know this one by heart. The Spartan woman arrived filthy and bleeding from her travels. We cared for her, gave her food, a bath, and she left. Where she went, I do not know. The child... could not be saved.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Who does know where she went?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: We've been spotted. Meet me later, near the Olive Tree of Herakles at the entrance of the sanctuary. I may have something for you.

speaker: Priest
en: And what do we have here, a priest and a mercenary out for a friendly stroll?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: May the gods be with you, Pleistos! I was just on my way to the archives when this misthios bumped into me.

speaker: Priest
en: Is that so? And what were you both chatting about so fervently, might I ask?

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm looking for my mother, a Spartan woman who came through here. This kind of priest brought me to this stone—it could be hers.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: I um, have to... There's something—I must be going.

speaker: Priest
en: We treat the sick, Eagle Bearer, and we respect the privacy of those we've treated. Now please leave. Your presence can only cause harm.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The tree of Herakles... I'm not sure if it's loved more for its legend or its olives. Now, where's that priest?

speaker: Kassandra
en: What happened? Who did this?

speaker: Priest
en: He knew the penalty for speaking with the Eagle Bearer about... her. Chrysis was clear.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You didn't have to kill him.

speaker: Priest
en: But we did... and now we'll kill you.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The good priest here was teaching me how to heal sword wounds.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Erm, yes... sword wounds...

speaker: Priest
en: Oh really? And what is the treatment for sword wounds according to Timoxenos here?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Um... snakes. You wrap snakes around the wound to stop the bleeding.

speaker: Priest
en: Ooh! A most ingenious treatment wouldn't you say, Timoxenos?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: I um, have to... There's something—I must be going.

speaker: Priest
en: We treat the sick, Eagle Bearer, and we respect the privacy of those we've treated. Now please leave. Your presence can only cause harm.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Um... olives. You stuff the wounds with olives—prevents bleeding.

speaker: Priest
en: Olives, that's a new one. Most impressive, Timoxenos.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: I um, have to... There's something—I must be going.

speaker: Priest
en: We treat the sick, Eagle Bearer, and we respect the privacy of those we've treated. Now please leave. Your presence can only cause harm.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Dogs.

speaker: Priest
en: What about them?

speaker: Kassandra
en: You use the dogs to lick the wounds clean.

speaker: Priest
en: Very good! Don't give away all our tricks, Timoxenos. Who will bring offerings to the gods when our patients learn to heal themselves?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: No, no, of course not. Now if you'll excuse me, I have matters to attend to.

speaker: Priest
en: You have your treatment, misthios. Now please leave the sanctuary.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The tree of Herakles... I'm not sure if it's loved more for its legend or its olives. Now, where's that priest?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: I thank you for your discretion, Eagle Bearer. Chrysis has many eyes and ears throughout the sanctuary.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What else can you tell me about the Spartan woman and child?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: The woman left the child's blanket behind. We tried to return it, but it was too painful a memory for her.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Where did she go? What happened to the child?

speaker: Spartan Baby Blanket
en: Old and worn, this is the very cloth Myrrine used to carry her injured baby.

speaker: Priest
en: So, Chrysis was right. You knew the rules, Timoxenos. You will suffer her wrath.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Pleistos, please!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Get behind me, priest. I'll deal with these two.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'm filthy and could use a good bath. The kind priest here was pointing me in the direction of the bath house.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Erm, yes... that's correct. The bath house is right over there. Now if you'll excuse me.

speaker: Priest
en: The baths are for healing the sick, not for washing the blood off one's hands. Leave.

speaker: Kassandra
en: The tree of Herakles... I'm not sure if it's loved more for its legend or its olives. Now, where's that priest?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: I thank you for your discretion, Eagle Bearer. Chrysis has many eyes and ears throughout the sanctuary.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What else can you tell me about the Spartan woman and child?

speaker: Timoxenos
en: The woman left the child's blanket behind. We tried to return it, but it was too painful a memory for her.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Where did she go? What happened to the child?

speaker: Spartan Baby Blanket
en: Old and worn, this is the very cloth Myrrine used to carry her injured baby.

speaker: Priest
en: So, Chrysis was right. You knew the rules, Timoxenos. You will suffer her wrath.

speaker: Timoxenos
en: Pleistos, please!

speaker: Kassandra
en: Get behind me, priest. I'll deal with these two.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Sokrates? You're... here.

speaker: Sokrates
en: I am!

speaker: Kassandra
en: What happened? The trial couldn't have taken place that quickly.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Had I been given the chance to defend myself, it would have been quick indeed. But unfortunately for me, I was let free before I could.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's good news.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Apparently those who had charges to bring against me were found dead, and evidence they claimed to have missing.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It sounds like someone was looking out for you.

speaker: Sokrates
en: There were also some people protesting my arrest, I was told. I have to ask... Did you have something to do with this?

speaker: Kassandra
en: Do you really need to ask?

speaker: Sokrates
en: No, but you still deserved the chance to answer.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Me? Kill? Steal? Arrange protests?

speaker: Sokrates
en: Yes.

speaker: Kassandra
en: It does sound like me, but it was someone else this time.

speaker: Sokrates
en: I'm glad I asked.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Did you have time to find an answer for the Pythia's words?

speaker: Sokrates
en: I thought it would have taken me much longer than it did, but the moment I stopped thinking about it, it came to me like a flash of Zeus's lightning.

speaker: Kassandra
en: So do you agree with the Pythia or not?

speaker: Sokrates
en: The Gods cannot lie, yet I know that I know nothing. I had to understand what it meant to for one who knows nothing to be called wise. I realized that though the Pythia said my name, she did not mean me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Who did she mean then?

speaker: Sokrates
en: That is not an answer I'd yet like to voice. It's one that people may not want to hear, and I must think on how I wish to share my new beliefs with Athens.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Whatever it is, be careful. I don't want to find you've been arrested again.

speaker: Kassandra
en: We should get you home. I'm sure you'll be more comfortable there.

speaker: Sokrates
en: In some ways, that will be true. In others... Well, Xanthippe will decide that.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Being free feels good, but I don't believe Xanthippe will be happy with me.

speaker: Kassandra
en: She has good reason to be mad this time.

speaker: Sokrates
en: We argue often about how I need to be careful with what I say and where I say it. This will only give her more cause to bring it up.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That doesn't sound very fun.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Oh, you misunderstand. I love it.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You do?

speaker: Sokrates
en: People see Xanthippe and believe it's her beauty that drew me to her, but it's her argumentative spirit I lust for.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Nobody ever likes that about me.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Having my opinions and thoughts challenged helps me refine them and to grow as a person.

speaker: Kassandra
en: And... she likes these arguments?

speaker: Sokrates
en: Oh, I doubt it. But it's in those fiery moments that her spirit is strongest, like an untamed horse.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Don't call her a horse to her face.

speaker: Sokrates
en: I'm afraid your advice is a bit too late.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Get somewhere safe, Sokrates!

speaker: Sokrates
en: I wonder what that was about.

speaker: Kassandra
en: With the things I do, it's sometimes hard to know.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Let's hurry back before anything else happens.

speaker: Xanthippe
en: You came back. Finally. I'm ready to return to Athens. I've had enough of Phokis and this talk of the Pythia.

speaker: Sokrates
en: You will be happy to hear I have no need for her words any longer.

speaker: Xanthippe
en: Then something positive came out of this after all.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I just remembered... a student of yours has been taking notes of your teachings. He wanted you to have them.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What did you do that for?

speaker: Sokrates
en: Nobody asked him to write down my words.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Even so, why not keep it? Share it with others.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Because of a story I was told as a boy.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Alright, let's hear it.

speaker: Sokrates
en: The king of Egypt, Thamus, was visited by the god Theuth. Theuth offered the invention of writing to the king and told him it was an elixir of memory and wisdom. But Thamus disagreed. He believed the people would no longer use their memories, for they would simply read instead. These written words would not offer true wisdom, but only the appearance of such.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You don't want your words written down so others can't use them to pretend to be smart.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Much like creatures in a painting, the words sit there unmoving. If you ask them a question, they will preserve a solemn silence, and no matter how many times you ask, they will only ever say the same thing. They cannot defend their message.

speaker: Kassandra
en: That's the part you like. The defense of your words.

speaker: Sokrates
en: All who speak should defend their words if questioned about them. That is why I choose to speak and not write, that is why any words of mine that last beyond my final breath will be those that people choose to remember. Those words will be true wisdom, and not an illusion.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I've had my fill of stories.

speaker: Sokrates
en: Then I'll save it for another time, should it be relevant. But know I did it for a good reason, and it was my decision to make.

speaker: Kassandra
en: What's you plan now?

speaker: Sokrates
en: After I return to Athens, there is much I need to consider.

speaker: Kassandra
en: You'll be careful, right?

speaker: Sokrates
en: If I have to choose between saying nothing and staying safe, or speaking up and risking my life, the choice is easy.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I should get going. I'm glad you're free.

speaker: Sokrates
en: As am I. Although, if you'll allow me, there is something...

speaker: Kassandra
en: I doubt I could stop you.

speaker: Sokrates
en: We like to believe that action means progress, but it's control that's so truly desired. The more we do, the more control it seems we have, but the less we allow for others. If we grip too tightly, we'll find we've crushed what it is we were holding onto.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Meaning?

speaker: Sokrates
en: Meaning we must sometimes let life unfold without trying to influence the outcome.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I'll keep that in mind.

speaker: Kassandra
en: I almost forgot. In your letter, you said you had something to ask me. What was it?

speaker: Sokrates
en: You know, I've completely forgotten now. Take care, Kassandra.

speaker: Kassandra
en: Stay out of trouble, Sokrates.
